oneLiner.en: Moving through Baruch Sheamar to Mizmor LeSodah, the Rav explains that thanking Hashem for every detail of life is the highest praise, the one offering that will remain in the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav explains the words of Baruch Sheamar: Ha-Keil speaks of Hashem's bond with all creation, Av of His bond with the Jewish people, and HaRachaman of mercy that does not follow a person's deeds. Each Jew praises Hashem by his own level, and the Rav tells how the Bais Aharon compared a poritz's pleasure to a tzaddik's pleasure in Nishmas. Saying the songs of David HaMelech is a privilege, since David joins in, and he protests a recent public insult to David. He maps the words of Baruch Sheamar onto the whole order of davening, tells of Rabbi Asher's mighty Yechid Chai HaOlamim, and explains why Hashem's name itself is His greatest praise. Mizmor LeSodah comes first, the choicest taste after the brachah, because thanks will outlast all offerings. True hodaah means knowing one received more than his share, and in the end David calls the whole world to praise Hashem.

en: Ha-Keil refers to Hashem's relationship with all creation, Av to His relationship with the Jewish people, and HaRachaman to mercy that is not measured by a person's deeds.
Saying the songs of David HaMelech is a great privilege, since a tzaddik whose words are repeated joins in, so David sings along with those who daven.
Mizmor LeSodah comes right after the brachah of Baruch Sheamar because, like tasting the choicest food after a brachah, it is the most precious of the songs.
One must thank Hashem for every small thing, not only for great events, since every moment of life rests on His constant hashgachah and countless hidden miracles.
True hodaah means recognizing that one has received more than his share, not saying thanks as good manners.
Mizmor LeSodah belongs to the days of Moshiach, when all offerings and prayers will cease except the korban todah and praise of Hashem.

title.en: Ha-Keil, Av HaRachaman, and praise by each one's level

summary.en: The Rav explains Ha-Keil as Hashem's bond with all creation and Av HaRachaman as His fatherly mercy toward the Jewish people, not measured by deeds, and discusses the nusach 'hamehulal befi amo'. He explains that chassidim and avadim praise Hashem each by his level, and tells how the Bais Aharon compared a poritz's pleasure ride over sugar to a tzaddik's pleasure in saying Nishmas.

title.en: Singing together with David HaMelech

summary.en: On 'uveshirei Dovid avdecha', the Rav explains that David's soul is the greatest, and since a tzaddik's lips move in the grave when his words are repeated, David sings along with us. He protests a recent public insult to David HaMelech in Eretz Yisrael and says a Jew should sing David's songs all the more with pride and joy.

title.en: From shevachos to Yechid Chai HaOlamim

summary.en: The Rav shows how the words of Baruch Sheamar point to the whole order of davening, from Mizmor LeSodah through Shemoneh Esrei, and explains Yechid Chai HaOlamim. He tells how Rabbi Asher's Yechid Chai HaOlamim was heard a mile away, and explains why, unlike a king, Hashem's own name is His greatest praise.

title.en: Why Mizmor LeSodah comes first

summary.en: The Rav explains that Mizmor LeSodah was composed for the korban todah, which is why it is omitted on Erev Pesach and Erev Yom Kippur. It comes first after the brachah like the choicest fruit after a brachah, or the tasting of Shabbos food on Erev Shabbos, and it belongs to the days of Moshiach when only the todah will remain.

title.en: Thanks that can never suffice

summary.en: The Rav calls thanks the most important bond between a creation and his Creator, bringing Nishmas to show that no praise is enough even for one kindness. He cites the Mishnah Berurah that kavanah is needed at Modim as at Avos, and says one must accustom himself to praise Hashem for every small thing, for every breath.

title.en: Hashgachah in every detail of the body

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yesod VeShoresh HaAvodah, who thanked Hashem even for finding his snuff box, and says a person who stumbles should first thank Hashem, since Hashem watches each person like a baby. He describes the countless parts of the body that could fail at any moment, cites 'ein ba'al haneis makir beniso', and brings the Tomer Devorah that Hashem gives strength even to one who sins.

title.en: Hodaah, Yehudah and the end of days

summary.en: From 've'ish lefi mehalelo' the Rav explains that a person is measured by his praise of Hashem, which is why kingship came from Yehudah, named for Leah's thanks. Following Rashi, true hodaah is knowing one took more than his share, as Yaakov said 'katonti'. He then brings Chazal that only the todah will remain, R. Samson Raphael Hirsch that Mizmor LeSodah closes Moshe Rabbeinu's eleven psalms, and notes it is the hundredth psalm.

title.en: Hari'u: a tzaddik's word moves the world

summary.en: On 'hari'u laShem kol ha'aretz' the Rav explains, with the Nefesh HaChaim, that man is the soul of the world, so a tzaddik like David can awaken all mankind to praise Hashem. He brings Rashi and the Ramban on the sign 'pakod pakadti' and an answer that words entering the heart are the sign of the redeemer, and argues that the Rambam's Moshiach, who needs no signs, is greater, since one word of his will move all of Klal Yisrael.

oneLiner.en: On Mizmor L'Sodah, the Rav explains that serving Hashem with simcha grows out of clear emunah and bitachon, the very thing Amalek attacks with doubt, and that only such joyful service survives a test.

abstract.en: The Rav continues with the second verse of Mizmor L'Sodah, 'Ivdu es Hashem b'simcha', and ties simcha to emunah. Amalek, whose name equals safek (doubt) in gematria, wages constant war on Jewish faith, and in this polluted, lowest generation, like Adar, the lowest month, doubts come easily. Simcha is the opposite of doubt: the one with clear emunah and bitachon is joyful, as a poor young man showed with his 'two cows', two verses of trust. The Megillah teaches that nothing is chance. The tochacha came because Hashem was served without simcha, and routine Judaism collapsed at the first test in America. The Ruzhiner's story shows learning every word of Gemara as holy. 'Hu asanu v'lo anachnu' teaches that Hashem makes a person and guides His people like a shepherd. Entering with thanks leads to tehillah, and a hundred brachos with amen strengthen emunah.

en: Serving Hashem with simcha depends on emunah: simcha is the security of a person who has no doubts, while doubt is Amalek's weapon.
The Megillah, which never mentions Hashem's name, teaches that every event is guided by hashgacha pratis and nothing happens by chance.
Judaism kept only out of routine and tradition, without simcha, does not withstand a test, as seen in the immigrants who worked on Shabbos in America.
'Hu asanu v'lo anachnu' means that Hashem, not a person's own wisdom or effort, makes him and his success.
One who enters Hashem's gates with thanks, even for the smallest step, merits to enter His courtyards with tehillah, a higher level.
The hundred daily brachos, answered with amen, are the 'hundred gates' through which a person enters emunah and draws down blessing.

title.en: Simcha rests on emunah; Amalek's war on faith

summary.en: The Rav opens with 'Ivdu es Hashem b'simcha' and says simcha comes from emunah, which Amalek constantly fights by casting doubts. He compares the spiritual pollution of the world to its physical pollution and says this is why doubts enter Jewish minds so easily today, though they are only a test to be fought.

title.en: Adar, the lowest month, and the end of exile

summary.en: The Rav explains why Amalek counted Adar as his month: as the last month it corresponds to the last, lowest generations, the heel before Moshiach. He compares the end of the Babylonian exile, when Achashverosh celebrated because seventy years had seemingly passed, to today, and notes that Amalek equals safek in gematria.

title.en: Simcha as certainty: the two cows and the Megillah

summary.en: The Rav says one with clear emunah and bitachon is joyful, and tells of a poor young man whose 'two cows' were two verses of trust. He then explains that the Megillah, where Hashem's name is not even mentioned, teaches that nothing is mikreh (chance), the claim of Amalek, and that simcha is the opposite of doubt.

title.en: Without simcha, routine fails the test

summary.en: The Rav brings Reb Chaim Vital that the Arizal reached his revelations through simcha, and the verse at the end of the tochacha that it came because Hashem was not served with simcha. He explains that service out of routine collapses at a test, as with immigrants to America who worked on Shabbos and whose descendants lost everything Jewish, and calls for chiyus in davening and learning.

title.en: The Ruzhiner and every word of Gemara

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Ruzhiner remembered which Amora said a teaching when a scholar did not, explaining that for him 'amar Rava' was also part of the holy Gemara. He concludes that learning is the living word of Hashem instructing a person, and the test of service not done out of tradition is whether it is done with simcha.

title.en: 'Hu asanu v'lo anachnu': Hashem makes us

summary.en: The Rav explains 'Elokim' as the master of all forces, as at Eliyahu's confrontation with the Baal, and 'hu asanu v'lo anachnu' as rejecting the idea of 'making a living' or a self-made career, which he compares to Pharaoh's boast. With Rashi he explains that Hashem made us before we existed, fixing a person's talents, match and livelihood before birth.

title.en: His people and His flock, even against the enemies

summary.en: The Rav says that whatever Haman, Amalek, Hitler or today's antisemites claim, the Jews are Hashem's people. He contrasts the Zionist hope that a land would end antisemitism, relating a prediction of Reb Chaim via Rav Sorotzkin, with the certainty that Hashem runs history, and reads 'v'lo' with a vav and the shepherd of Tehillim 23 as assurance.

title.en: Entering with thanks, then with tehillah

summary.en: The Rav describes the Jew of real emunah who rejoices at being able to stand a test, and explains 'bo'u she'arav b'sodah': one should enter shul, the beis medrash and Shabbos thanking Hashem for being let in, as an old Stoliner chassid taught. Through thanks for even the smallest step one reaches the courtyards 'bis'hilah', a higher praise, as Ashrei begins with Tehillah L'Dovid.

title.en: A hundred brachos, a hundred gates of emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the sefarim that 'she'arav' are the hundred daily brachos, parallel to the hundred sockets of the Mishkan, and explains that one hundred is the domain of the Samech-Mem, while 101 goes beyond it. A brachah is complete with amen, and through the amens, 'shomer emunim', one enters the hundred gates and draws down blessing.

catalogTitle: המשך מזמור לתודה - עניני שמחה ואמונה

oneLiner.en: Continuing Mizmor l'Sodah, the Rav explains Adar as the hidden, lowest month in which Hashem's name is incomplete, how answering amen and amen yehei shmei rabbah restores it, and why the test of the last generations is emunah alone.

abstract.en: The Rav returns to Mizmor l'Sodah and explains that, just as souls and places have a 'head' and a 'heel', Adar is the heel among the months: a month of concealment, like Persia (Eilam) and the Megillah, where Hashem's name does not appear. He brings the Gemara that answering amen yehei shmei rabbah with all one's strength tears up a decree of seventy years, and Tosafos' reading that it is a prayer for the incomplete name, hidden by Amalek and Haman, to become whole. Answering amen, from emunah, opens the hundred gates, and Mizmor l'Sodah, the hundredth psalm, enters them with thanks. He explains why Chanukah and Purim belong to Modim, tells of the souls who were told the remedy is emunah, shows the Megillah's chain of hidden miracles, and ends with guarding emunah from today's media and strengthening it through Torah.

en: Adar is the 'heel' of the months, a month of hiddenness like Eilam (Persia), where miracles are concealed in nature and Hashem's name does not appear in the Megillah.
Amen yehei shmei rabbah is a prayer that Hashem's name, made incomplete by Amalek and Haman's concealment, become whole, and Adar is a special time to put strength into it.
Answering amen, which comes from emunah, opens the hundred gates of heaven; Mizmor l'Sodah, the hundredth psalm, corresponds to the last of them and enters with thanks.
Chanukah and Purim, weekday festivals made for the galus, are mentioned in Modim, where one bows down, because the Shechinah comes down to the lowest places and the lowest Jews.
For the last generations the remedy is emunah alone; the whole matter of Purim is believing in Hashem and in hashgacha pratis.
Guarding emunah has two sides: avoiding literature and media that plant doubts, and strengthening it through deep, warm learning of Torah.

title.en: Adar, the hidden heel of the months

summary.en: Resuming Mizmor l'Sodah, the Rav explains from Sefer Yetzirah that place, time and soul each have a head and a heel: Nissan is the head and Adar the heel. Adar is like Eilam (Persia), a place of concealment, the time of Esther and hester panim, when Hashem's name is hidden in the Megillah.

title.en: Amen yehei shmei rabbah and the incomplete name

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that answering amen yehei shmei rabbah with all one's strength tears up a seventy-year decree, and links it to the end of the seventy years of galus Bavel under Persia. Through Tosafos and Rashi on 'ki yad al kes Yah' he explains that Amalek and Haman hide Hashem's name, and the prayer asks that it become whole.

title.en: Amen opens the hundred gates

summary.en: The Rav explains that amen means from beginning to end of all levels, and that whoever is careful with amen has all the gates opened for him, reading 'pischu she'arim' as the nation that answers amen. Amen comes from emunah, and Mizmor l'Sodah, the hundredth psalm, corresponds to the last of the hundred gates and enters them with thanks.

title.en: Hoda'ah, Modim and the weekday festivals

summary.en: The Rav explains hoda'ah as thanks for more than one's share, from Leah naming Yehudah, and calls Kislev and Adar months of hoda'ah. Torah festivals appear in Retzeh, the avodah of the Beis Hamikdash, while Chanukah and Purim, weekday festivals made for galus, appear in Modim where one bows down. He describes Jews on the levels of Shabbos, Yom Tov and Chol Hamoed.

title.en: Melacha as a curse; the Shechinah comes down

summary.en: The Rav explains that melacha is a curse: Adam before the sin did no work, and the thirty-nine curses became the thirty-nine melachos, which is why Shabbos, a source of blessing, has none. He lays out the levels of Jews by how much work they do, and explains that on Chanukah and Purim the Shechinah comes down to the lowest place, like a great man visiting the sick.

title.en: The souls told the remedy is emunah

summary.en: The Rav ties Adar to the heel before Moshiach and to the prayer for a whole name, and brings Chavakuk, who set all the mitzvos on 'tzaddik be'emunaso yichyeh'. He retells the story of a great disciple of the Ba'al Shem Tov's disciples: souls who kept returning in gilgulim with a failing mark went up level by level to Hashem, who told them the remedy is emunah.

title.en: Purim is emunah: the chain of hidden miracles

summary.en: The Rav explains that the whole matter of Purim is emunah and hashgacha pratis: every detail of the Megillah, from Vashti to Mordechai and Bigsan and Teresh, fits into one plan beyond chance, as the meforshim such as the Alshich and the Nesivos show. A person who wrote down his own life would see the same chain, as the Ramban at the end of Parshas Bo says.

title.en: Purim's seriousness and thanks for every detail

summary.en: The Rav says Adar is the time to strengthen emunah and to learn the Megillah with its meforshim, and brings the Chasam Sofer against treating Purim as frivolity: Purim is an awesome day like Yom Kippur. With a mashal of a president caring about every detail of a simple man's day, he explains the thanks of Modim for a life in Hashem's hand, and 'ki tov Hashem le'olam chasdo'.

title.en: Emunah down the generations; the Rambam's warning

summary.en: The Rav explains 'ad dor vador emunaso' as emunah tumbling down to the lowest generations until Moshiach, and says the test of our time is emunah, as the Chofetz Chaim said about a dybbuk. Guarding emunah has a sur mera and an aseh tov; for the first he brings the Rambam forbidding books that plant doubts, and asks why the precise Rambam adds 'many books'.

title.en: Today's media, and emunah through Torah

summary.en: The Rav answers that 'many books' includes all literature: newspapers, television and even radio news fill the mind with filth and doubts in emunah. For aseh tov he explains that deep, warm Torah learning shows its wonders and that it is from heaven, and preparing for Purim through it builds emunah. Where the ghetto once preserved Jews, today in free America they must mix and still hold on to emunah.

catalogTitle: Emunah - A Hereditary Instinct from the Avos

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's emunah is an inherited instinct, a piece of Avraham Avinu in every Yid that Hashem guards and that can never be lost, and that it comes through the mother as feeling rather than logic.

abstract.en: The Rav compares Avraham Avinu to a seed from which a whole tree grows: every Yid was once in Avraham, and Avraham is now in every Yid. Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the bracha Magen Avraham means that Hashem guards this point of emunah, which can be covered up but never extinguished; a kofer only covers it. Since every Yid has a beginning in Avraham, he also has an end, and he will return. He tells the story of the Ramban's student Avner, who found his name in the middle letters of a verse in Ha'azinu, and explains that only the middle, the temporary part of a Jew, can be lost. He then speaks of the Seder night, when emunah is implanted in children through words and through matzah, wine and the cups, and explains that emunah, being emotion and instinct, comes from the mother. He ends that inherited emunah is not yet the mitzvah of emunah.

en: Like every apple and leaf of a tree that was once in its seed, every Yid was once in Avraham Avinu, and a piece of Avraham is now in every Yid.
The bracha Magen Avraham means that Hashem shields the point of Avraham's emunah in every Yid, so that it can never be extinguished, only covered up.
Whatever has a beginning has an end; since every Yid begins in Avraham, he will ultimately return to his roots and do teshuvah.
On the Seder night emunah is implanted in children, both through telling of Yetzias Mitzrayim and through eating matzah, which the Zohar calls the food of emunah.
Emunah is instinct and feeling rather than logic, and therefore, unlike other traits, it is determined by the mother.
Inherited, instinctive emunah is one way of having emunah, but it is not yet the fulfillment of the mitzvah of emunah.

title.en: A piece of Avraham Avinu in every Yid

summary.en: The Rav compares Avraham Avinu to a seed that holds the whole tree, and explains with the Chiddushei HaRim that Magen Avraham means Hashem guards this point of emunah in every Yid. A kofer only covers it up; since every Yid has a beginning in Avraham he has an end, and when Mashiach comes the hidden spark will flare up.

title.en: The Ramban and his student Avner

summary.en: The Rav tells the story brought in the Kav HaYashar of the Ramban's student Avner, who left Yiddishkeit and challenged the Ramban to show him where he is alluded to in Ha'azinu. The Ramban found his name in the third letters of a verse that speaks of erasing their memory, and Avner did teshuvah and set out to sea in a boat without oars.

title.en: Why the middle letters: a Yid is never lost

summary.en: The Rav asks why the hint was in the middle letters, when one normally reads first or last letters, which contain the whole word. He explains that every Yid has a beginning in Avraham and therefore an end that returns to it, like the Torah reading that starts again from Bereishis; only the middle, the temporary part, can be lost, so even Avner will come back.

title.en: The Avos as a new beginning and the Seder night

summary.en: The Rav recalls that the Avos and Imahos could not have children because they were a new species cut off from the previous generations. He then explains that the Seder night was formed as the night to instill emunah in children, since Yetzias Mitzrayim, in which the Ten Utterances of creation were replayed backwards in the Ten Plagues, is the foundation of emunah.

title.en: Matzah and wine: logic and feeling

summary.en: The Rav explains that eating matzah, the food of emunah, internalizes emunah, and that the three matzos correspond to the Avos and the four cups to the Imahos, like the shin of three and four heads on the tefillin. Wheat brings knowledge while wine brings feeling; men lean to logic and women to emotion, and emunah is feeling and instinct.

title.en: Emunah comes from the mother

summary.en: Through a rule of dikduk, dropping the final nun of a root to form a noun, the Rav shows that from 'amen', to believe, comes 'em', mother. Everything else is determined by the father, but Jewishness follows the mother, because emunah is instinct like the spider's web or the beaver's dam. He ends that this inherited emunah, which Magen Avraham guards, is not yet the mitzvah of emunah, to be discussed next time.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Ashrei is so great a praise: Hashem feeds every creature in a perfectly balanced order, He is a personal G-d who fills every small need, and each day He gives a new blessing.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that whoever says Tehillah l'David three times a day is assured of the World to Come, because it is arranged by the alef-beis and contains 'Pose'ach es yadecha'. He asks what is so wonderful about feeding all creatures, and answers that only habit hides the wonder: every creature gets its own food, and all of nature is held in a precise balance, which the alef-beis order hints at. He then explains why we first say 'Ashrei yoshvei veisecha': one must settle oneself before davening. A story of the Toldos Yaakov Yosef and Eliyahu Hanavi teaches 'ashrei ha'am shekachah lo' as accepting everything as hashgachah pratis. He explains 'Elokai haMelech' as two relationships, the general King and the personal G-d, and 'bechol yom avarcheka' as giving Hashem strength to bestow good, new every day and every Shabbos.

en: Only habit keeps people from seeing the wonder that every creature in the world receives its own food in its own place.
The alef-beis order of Ashrei hints at the precise order and balance with which Hashem provides parnassah to all of creation.
Before davening one must sit and settle one's mind, and after davening not run off; this is why Tehillah l'David is preceded by 'Ashrei yoshvei veisecha'.
'Elokai haMelech' expresses two relationships with Hashem: the King of the whole world, and one's personal G-d to whom one turns for every small thing.
Every day and every Shabbos brings a new blessing and new tikkunim; nothing in davening is a repetition.

title.en: Why Ashrei earns the World to Come

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that one who says Tehillah l'David three times daily is a ben olam haba, because of its alef-beis and 'Pose'ach es yadecha'. He asks what is so great about feeding all creatures when people and animals sometimes die of hunger.

title.en: The wonder hidden by habit

summary.en: The Rav explains that we take for granted what would amaze us if it happened once in a lifetime, like the sunrise. Every creature gets its own food, animals prepare for winter, and only a famine makes headlines; he brings the Chasam Sofer on the generation of the desert seeing bread grow from the ground.

title.en: Hunger as a decree; nature's balance

summary.en: The Rav explains that when someone dies of hunger it is a specific decree from Heaven, like any illness, while the general order is that every creature has food. He describes how worms, birds and birds of prey keep each other in proportion, a balance unchanged for thousands of years that only man can disturb.

title.en: Parnassah with an alef-beis

summary.en: The Rav concludes that this is the meaning of Ashrei: each creature desires its own food, which serves several purposes in its habitat, and the alef-beis signifies that parnassah comes with order. Tehillah l'David is a song of amazement, and one who contemplates it three times a day rather than by rote is a ben olam haba.

title.en: Settling the mind before davening

summary.en: The Rav explains why Tehillah l'David is preceded by 'Ashrei yoshvei veisecha': the Gemara says the early chassidim waited an hour before and after davening, learning it from this pasuk and from 'yeshvu yesharim es panecha'. He adds that one should begin with simchah and security in Hashem, and that 'Ashrei' is the foremost of the expressions of praise in Tehillim.

title.en: The Toldos and 'zol zain azoi'

summary.en: After explaining the second Ashrei, 'Ashrei ha'am shekachah lo', the Rav tells how the Toldos Yaakov Yosef, upset at not being waited for at a bris, saw a guest answer everything with 'zol zain azoi'. It was revealed to be Eliyahu Hanavi teaching him that everything is hashgachah pratis, and the Toldos explained the pasuk accordingly.

title.en: Elokai haMelech: two relationships

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'tehillah' is a very high level of praise and translates 'Aromimcha'. 'HaMelech' is Hashem as the general King, like a president one would not ask for bananas, while 'Elokai' is the personal G-d one turns to for everything; he illustrates with Reb Nachum of Chernobyl praying that a maid should not leave.

title.en: Elokai written full: no empty space

summary.en: The Rav points out that 'Elokai' here is written full, with a vav, meaning there is no empty space in a person's life that is not Hashem's concern, down to a toothpick after a meal. 'Va'avarchah shimcha l'olam va'ed' means that through this praise one merits praising Hashem in the World to Come.

title.en: Bechol yom avarcheka: a new blessing daily

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'avarcheka' truly means blessing Hashem, giving Him strength to bestow good, as in Rabbi Yishmael's blessing in the Kodesh Hakodashim. Every day has its own blessing and tikkun, as the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah built the prayers to carry new meanings each day; he brings the Shelah's 600,000 Shabbosos, each Jew having his own Shabbos and his own letter in the Torah.

oneLiner.en: On the words of Ashrei, 'Gadol Hashem… v'ligdulaso ein cheker', the Rav explains that Hashem cannot be grasped by investigation but is known through the neshamah, the mesorah of Sinai, the tzaddikim of every generation and the beauty of His world.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the verse 'Gadol Hashem u'mehulal me'od, v'ligdulaso ein cheker' and explains that each sense grasps its own kind of thing, and the intellect is not the faculty that grasps Hashem. Every Jew has a neshamah and a measure of ruach hakodesh, blocked only by sin; Klal Yisroel as a whole has it, which is why its minhagim are true, as the Binas Adam and Rav Moshe Feinstein show. The human mind was made for the physical world; Hashem is felt through Torah, mitzvos and kedushah. The Torah never proves the ikkarim by investigation: they rest on what an entire nation saw at Sinai, as the Yismach Moshe writes. On 'dor l'dor yeshabach ma'asecha' he explains that the tzaddikim of each generation reveal Hashem, with stories of Lechovitch, Belz and the Satmar Rav's megillah, and that later generations understand Hashem's ways. He ends with 'hadar kevod hodecha': the grace and beauty of creation.

en: Each sense grasps its own kind of thing, and the intellect with its investigation is not the faculty through which a person grasps Hashem.
Every Jew has a neshamah that is a part of G-d and a potential for ruach hakodesh; sin insulates him from it, and Klal Yisroel as a whole has ruach hakodesh, so its minhagim are true.
The human mind was made only for the physical world; Hashem is felt through Torah, mitzvos, honesty and kedushah, not through calculation.

The Torah never brings proofs from investigation for its foundations; Jewish belief rests on the experience of an entire nation at Yetzias Mitzrayim and Sinai, handed down from generation to generation.
'Dor l'dor yeshabach ma'asecha': the tzaddikim of each generation are Hashem's handiwork, through whom His praise is told.
What one generation cannot understand of Hashem's ways becomes clear to later generations, as with the rebuilding of Torah after the destruction in Europe.
'Hadar kevod hodecha': Hashem made the world with grace and beauty beyond what was needed, and for this one must thank and praise Him.

title.en: Gadol Hashem: no investigating His greatness

summary.en: After a few words on the nusach of tefillah set by the Anshei Knesses Hagedolah, the Rav takes up the verse 'Gadol Hashem… v'ligdulaso ein cheker'. He explains that each sense grasps its own kind of thing, a picture with the eyes and a symphony with the ears, and that the intellect is not the faculty for grasping Hashem.

title.en: The neshamah and the ruach hakodesh of Klal Yisroel

summary.en: Citing the Kuzari, the Rav explains that every Jew has a neshamah and a measure of ruach hakodesh, and only sin insulates him from it; the neshamah knows what lies beyond walls and time. Klal Yisroel as a whole has ruach hakodesh, which is why its minhagim are true, as he shows from the Binas Adam and a teshuvah of Rav Moshe Feinstein.

title.en: The mind cannot reach Hashem; emunah through Torah and mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav explains that the human mind was made for the physical world and breaks down on questions of infinite time and space; Hashem is felt through Torah, mitzvos and kedushah. He discusses the old dispute over chakirah, says that today one should not engage in it, and stresses that the Torah never proves its ikkarim by investigation, unlike religions that believe 'because he said so'.

title.en: A whole nation saw: the mesorah of Sinai

summary.en: The Rav brings the pesukim in Devarim that no nation ever heard Hashem speak from the fire, and explains that something an entire people witnessed and handed down cannot be denied. He reads a teshuvah of the Yismach Moshe on doubts in emunah, compares denial of Sinai to denying the Holocaust or Julius Caesar, and explains that the nations too accept the Torah's miracles.

title.en: Dor l'dor: the tzaddikim as Hashem's handiwork

summary.en: Returning to the verse, the Rav explains that Hashem's greatness is known not through philosophy but through the mesorah, 'dor l'dor yeshabach ma'asecha', and warns that every Jew must guard his emunah. He brings the Zohar on Shavuos night that 'ma'asecha' and 'ma'aseh yadav' are the tzaddikim, and describes Jews whose avodah radiates onto others.

title.en: Lechovitch, Belz and the Satmar Rav's megillah

summary.en: The Rav tells how a poritz listening to the Lechovitcher daven said that his love for his wife was nothing next to the Jew's love for Hashem, and how the young R' Shalom of Belz told the megillah in Lublin. He describes hearing the Satmar Rav read the megillah for two hours, brings the Chasam Sofer and Kedushas Levi on the light of the megillah, and his shout at 'hakerovim v'harechokim'.

title.en: The falling generations, and what later generations understand

summary.en: With the example of a falling stone that speeds up as it drops, the Rav explains that the decline between generations grows ever greater, so earlier tzaddikim are beyond compare. Then, with other meforshim, he reads 'dor l'dor' as later generations understanding what Hashem did, bringing the Chazon Ish's mashal of the tailor cutting silk after the destruction in Europe.

title.en: Hadar kevod hodecha: the beauty of creation

summary.en: On 'hadar kevod hodecha', the Rav describes the beauty of the countryside that the city hides, and explains 'hazan es ha'olam… b'chen' : Hashem could have fed people like a car with fuel, but made food beautiful, varied and tasty, for which one must thank and praise Him. He ends with the ever-changing clouds and his love of speaking about Hashem's wonders.

catalogTitle: The Wonders of the World Point to a Creator

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that the wonders of creation, down to the human body, plainly point to a Maker, and that denial of Him comes from rationalization, not from knowledge.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by recalling that emunah is an inheritance from the Avos and that a Jew believes instinctively unless he tries to deny it. Such denial is rationalization: Esav blamed his wives for losing the brachos, idol worshippers sought permission for forbidden relations, and Chazal read 'do not stray after your heart and your eyes' as heresy and immorality, because lust leads a person to justify himself with kefirah. He tells the story he once told ten-year-olds about two Africans who explained a watch with bugs chasing cheese, likening it to scientists' changing theories, while the Maker's own account is in the Torah. The kashas are weak; the Chovos Halevavos's mashal of a painting made by a splash of paint shows the absurdity, and Dovid HaMelech sings of creation's wonders. From the human body, the foot and the S-shaped spine, one sees the Creator. He ends with a Yemenite woman who doubted a spaceship, showing there is no conflict between absolute knowledge and Torah, only between theories and Torah.

en: A Jew believes in Hashem instinctively; denial comes only when he tries to deny it.
Kefirah is rationalization: a person who wants to follow his desires looks for a justification and finds it in denying the Torah.
Scientists' theories of how the world came about keep changing, while the Maker Himself wrote the account of creation in the Torah.
Every part of the world, and every detail of the human body, shows that there is a Maker who made it and controls it.
There is no contradiction between absolute scientific knowledge and the Torah, only between changing theories and the Torah.

title.en: Denial as rationalization

summary.en: The Rav recalls that emunah is inherited from the Avos and that a Jew believes instinctively. He shows that denial is rationalization: Esav blamed his wives for losing the brachos, and Chazal read 'after your heart and your eyes' as heresy and immorality, since desire leads a person to justify himself with kefirah.

title.en: The Africans and the watch

summary.en: The Rav tells the story he once told ten-year-olds who had been taught evolution: two Africans explained a watch with bugs chasing cheese and 'proved' it by hearing them stamp. He likens this to scientists who publish ever-changing theories of how the world came by itself.

title.en: The Maker's own book and the painting

summary.en: As Rabbi Pinkus told the Africans to read the watchmaker's book, the Rav says the Maker wrote the account of creation in Sefer Bereishis, but people avoid it because it obligates them. The kashas are weak; he brings the Chovos Halevavos's mashal of a masterpiece made by a splash of paint, and Dovid HaMelech's song of the wonders of creation.

title.en: Seeing the Creator in the human body

summary.en: Citing Iyov's 'from my flesh I see G-d', the Rav describes a diagram of the foot at a doctor's office and an anatomy textbook full of wonders, and explains why the spine is shaped like an S. Medicine assumes everything in the body has a purpose; such wonders cannot come from an explosion.

title.en: The Yemenite woman and the spaceship

summary.en: The Rav tells of a Yemenite Jewish woman who denied the first spaceship because the gates of heaven are in Yerushalayim, having not learned Rashi. He concludes that absolute knowledge never conflicts with the Torah, only theories do, and that denying the Creator is rationalization by people too weak to keep the Torah.

oneLiner.en: Learning the verses of Ashrei from 'Ve'ezuz nora'osecha' onward, the Rav explains that Dovid HaMelech sees Hashem's mercy and hashgachah in every small thing, and that a person who believes this can turn suffering into delight.

abstract.en: The Rav learns Tehillim 145 verse by verse. Others speak of Hashem's might when something extraordinary happens, but Dovid HaMelech sees His greatness in a leaf or a feather, and a small act done for avodas Hashem counts more in Heaven than events that make history. Hashem is gracious and slow to anger: He waits for the wicked and even gives them strength, hoping they will return. His mercy is on all His creatures, shown in stories of Rebbi and the calf, the Arizal and the chickens, and the Ba'al Shem Tov and the worm. The Rav explains the great destruction fifty years earlier as Hashem gathering damaged souls for their tikkun, like leftovers mixed into a kugel, and tells stories of the Malach, the Sadigura Rebbe and the Beis Aharon showing that everything has a reckoning. Whoever believes in hashgachah pratis sweetens his suffering: nega becomes oneg, as on Shabbos. He ends with 'Yoducha' and the levels of tzaddikim and chassidim.

en: Dovid HaMelech does not need wonders to see Hashem; he sees His greatness and His connection to every small thing in the world.
Hashem's patience goes beyond waiting: He keeps giving the sinner life and strength, even to keep sinning, so that he may still do teshuvah.
Hashem's mercy extends to every creature, down to a single worm, and every Jew must know that all He does is with mercy and kindness.
Everything that happens to a person has an exact reckoning, often a tikkun of a former life, which no human calculation can grasp.
A person who recognizes that his suffering comes from Hashem through hashgachah pratis sweetens the judgments, so that the greatest suffering can shrink to a trifle.
The same letters can turn nega (affliction) into oneg (delight), and this is the secret of Shabbos, on which a Jew testifies that Hashem created everything.

title.en: Seeing Hashem in every small thing

summary.en: On 'Ve'ezuz nora'osecha' and 'Zecher rav tuvcha', the Rav explains that others praise Hashem when something awesome happens, but Dovid HaMelech sees Him in a leaf or a feather. A bottle of milk bought to daven better makes a greater impression in Heaven than events that make the newspapers.

title.en: Gracious, slow to anger and great in kindness

summary.en: The Rav explains why the wicked prosper while tzaddikim are judged to a hair's breadth: Hashem waits for teshuvah. Beyond that, as 'great in kindness', He even gives the sinner strength to continue, as if handing more stones to someone throwing stones at Him.

title.en: His mercy is on all His creatures

summary.en: On 'Tov Hashem lakol', the Rav tells of Rebbi and the calf, the Arizal and the chickens, and the Ba'al Shem Tov and the worm in the heat, showing that Hashem has mercy on every creature, and says every Jew must know that all He does is with mercy.

title.en: The destruction and the kugel of souls

summary.en: The Rav addresses the great destruction of Klal Yisrael fifty years earlier: Hashem gathers souls from the generations of the Flood and the Dispersion into one generation before Moshiach, like a housewife mixing Shabbos leftovers into a kugel, and their suffering is a light judgment compared to what they deserved.

title.en: The Malach and the two neighbors

summary.en: The Rav tells of two neighbors who came to the Malach, one with a bad wife and one with poor parnassah. Through the verse in Iyov about three chances, he explains that such a hard life lets a soul return to the world for its tikkun.

title.en: The mezuzah in Sadigura and the Beis Aharon

summary.en: The Rav tells of a chassid whom the Sadigura Rebbe kept from moving, who died after affixing his mezuzah with kavanah, and of a man whose wife tormented him, whom the Beis Aharon sent home, after which he suffered in the street instead. Both show that everything comes with a reckoning.

title.en: Believing sweetens the suffering

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's measure of suffering, a nickel instead of a quarter, and the Bnei Yissaschar: one who acknowledges that suffering comes from Hashem turns great suffering into a trifle. He explains that nega becomes oneg through the letters, and that one should daven for the judgments to be sweetened for himself, his family and all Yisrael.

title.en: The metzora's nega and the oneg of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav reads 'the nega did not turn its ayin' as the nega not becoming oneg, and explains that Shabbos, on which a Jew testifies that Hashem created everything, is the secret of turning nega into oneg and pesha into shefa.

title.en: Yoducha: Your works and Your chassidim

summary.en: On 'Yoducha Hashem kol ma'asecha', the Rav explains that the soul praises Hashem with every breath, that tzaddikim are called His 'handiwork' and adorn the Torah on Shavuos night, and that chassidim are a higher level who bring blessing into the Shechinah. He closes by announcing a break to learn about Pesach.

oneLiner.en: Through the pesukim of Ashrei from 'vachasidecha yevarchucha' to 'somech Hashem', the Rav explains how Klal Yisroel blesses Hashem, why Hashem's rule over each generation differs, and why today's generation is tested above all in emunah.

abstract.en: The Rav explains that all of creation praises Hashem by its very existence, but only Klal Yisroel, the 'chasidim' of the world, can bless Him: their mitzvos and brachos bring strength and shefa (flow of blessing) into the upper worlds, as Rabbi Yishmael was asked to bless Hashem in the Kodesh HaKodashim. Such a blessing must follow the fixed nusach of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, with Hashem's name and His kingship, which is the meaning of 'kevod malchuscha yomeru'. Yet all the praises only make His might known to people. 'Malchuscha' speaks of space, 'memshalt'cha' of time: in each generation Hashem rules with a different purpose, and the task of this generation is emunah. The Rav describes a world stripped of kingship and of fear, set up so that believing is hard, and brings stories about the fear of a king. Emunah is drawn from Yetzias Mitzrayim, which Hashem showed once and which is handed down. He ends with the missing nun of Ashrei and 'somech Hashem'.

en: All creatures praise Hashem by existing, but only the Jewish people, the 'chasidim' among the nations, can bless Him and bring shefa into all the worlds through their mitzvos and brachos.

Because a Jew's blessing opens the upper worlds, it must follow the nusach of the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, where every word is weighed by pshat, remez, drush and sod, and it needs Hashem's name and His kingship.
All the praises of Hashem only make His might known to people as far as they can grasp; no person, angel or seraph can reach the end of His praise.
'Malchuscha' is Hashem's kingship across all worlds, in space; 'memshalt'cha' is His governance in time, which changes from generation to generation according to each generation's tikkun.
The task of the present generation, before Moshiach, is emunah, and the world is deliberately set up without kingship or fear so that believing will be a real test.
Emunah is drawn from Yetzias Mitzrayim, which the whole people saw; Hashem showed it once and does not repeat it for every generation, and it is handed down by mesorah.

title.en: Only Klal Yisroel can bless Hashem

summary.en: On 'yoducha Hashem kol maasecha vachasidecha yevarchucha', the Rav explains that all creation praises Hashem by existing, while the Jewish people, the 'chasidim' among the nations, bless Him and bring shefa into the worlds, like Rabbi Yishmael who was asked to bless Hashem in the Kodesh HaKodashim.

title.en: Kevod malchuscha: the fixed nusach of a brachah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew's praise opens the upper worlds, so after prophecy ended the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah fixed a nusach in which every word is measured. A brachah needs Hashem's name and kingship, and this is 'kevod malchuscha yomeru'; he brings Tosafos on how Shemoneh Esrei has malchus.

title.en: Praise only to make His might known

summary.en: The Rav explains 'lehodia livnei ha'adam gevurosav': all the praises fixed by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah and David HaMelech cannot reach the end of Hashem's praise, and only show people His might as far as they can grasp. He calls the pasuk a parenthesis in the middle of the alef-beis of Ashrei.

title.en: Malchus in space, memshalah in time

summary.en: On 'malchuscha malchus kol olamim umemshalt'cha bechol dor vador', the Rav distinguishes a king from a ruler, as with Yosef in Mitzrayim, and explains that kingship speaks of space while governance speaks of time. Each generation has its own task, and the task of today's generation is emunah.

title.en: A generation tested in emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chofetz Chaim that before Moshiach the test is emunah, and the uncensored Rambam that even the founder of Christianity prepared the world for the idea of Moshiach. He tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov leaving a wagon driver who did not cross himself, explains that heresy is worse than idolatry, and describes a world without fear of kingship.

title.en: Fear of a king, then and now

summary.en: The Rav tells of a chassid of the Ba'al HaTanya who learned how to daven from a soldier flogged for frozen ears, and of Czar Nikolai's old soldier whose service warmed his blood. He explains that people once feared a king and so feared the Day of Judgment, while today there is no kingship and no religion, so that the Jews' emunah will be tested.

title.en: Each generation adds its part; the tzaddik rules

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch that each generation contributes something whose purpose is seen only generations later, when Hashem's hand as captain becomes clear. From Chassidic sefarim he adds that 'memshalt'cha' is the tzaddik who rules through fear of Heaven, found in every generation.

title.en: Emunah from Yetzias Mitzrayim; somech Hashem

summary.en: In the days of Sefirah the Rav explains that emunah is drawn from Yetzias Mitzrayim, where the ten makos matched the ten maamaros and led to the ten dibros. He tells of Reb Elchonon Wasserman and a musician's 'concert' to explain why Hashem does not repeat miracles for every generation, then explains why the nun is missing in Ashrei and 'somech Hashem' comes first.

oneLiner.en: Learning the pesukim of Ashrei from 'Somech Hashem' onward, the Rav explains how Hashem raises the fallen even through a tzaddik's fall, how His hashgacha pratis provides every creature's food at its time, why one must daven for parnassa, and why no tefilah is ever lost.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara's question why Ashrei has no verse for the letter nun: it would speak of falling, and words have power, so David wrote 'Somech Hashem lechol hanoflim' instead, which the sefarim read as Hashem Himself raising Knesses Yisrael. He warns against criticizing tzaddikim: Hashem sometimes lets a tzaddik fall so he can reach and raise low souls, as the Midrash on Yosef and the brothers and the story of the Bach's sneeze show. On 'Einei chol' he contrasts the Rambam's view of hashgacha pratis with the Ba'al Shem Tov's, citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the bird, and tells stories of provision arriving exactly when needed. On 'Poseach es yadecha' he explains the duty to daven for parnassa (the Strelisker and the Ruzhiner) and tefilah as an exercise in emunah. He ends with the Ba'al Shem Tov's water carrier and the teaching that every tefilah is answered, if need be stored for later generations, as with Avraham's tefilah for Sodom.

en: David left the nun out of Ashrei because it would speak of falling, and a person's words have the power to draw down good or, chas veshalom, harm.
When a tzaddik falls it is part of Hashem's plan, so that he can go down to a low place and raise souls from there; one must not criticize tzaddikim.
According to the Ba'al Shem Tov, hashgacha pratis reaches every detail of creation, down to how a single straw falls, and every creature receives its food exactly at its time.
A Jew must ask Hashem for parnassa; tefilah is an exercise in emunah, because the very asking awakens him to recognize that Hashem is the provider.
Even when a harsh decree has been set, Hashem's attribute of mercy can sweeten and neutralize it: 'tzaddik' in His decree and 'chasid' in all His deeds.
Every tefilah is answered; when it seems unanswered it is stored in the heavenly account for later, for the person, his children or future generations.

title.en: Why Ashrei has no nun

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's question why there is no nun verse in Ashrei and explains that falling may not be spoken of because speech has great power. He then brings a parable from the sefarim of a king who calls back his banished queen, read into 'Somech Hashem': Hashem Himself will raise Knesses Yisrael.

title.en: When a tzaddik falls

summary.en: The Rav warns against criticizing gedolei Yisrael and explains that Hashem sometimes makes a tzaddik fall so that he can repair low places. He brings Tzelafchad, a saying of Rebbe Nachman of Breslov about two mistakes people make, and the Midrash on Yosef and the brothers that 'nora alila' shows everything followed a plan.

title.en: The Bach's sneeze and Gehinom

summary.en: Discussing why the Ba'al Shem Tov did not hold stringently on chadash, the Rav tells how, after the Bach's passing, no sin was found on him until an angel brought a sneeze that startled an animal and moved a wagon; Gehinom was cooled for him, and when he left he took the wicked out with him. This, he concludes, is how Hashem raises the fallen through a tzaddik.

title.en: 'Einei chol': hashgacha pratis on every creature

summary.en: On 'Einei chol eilecha yesaberu' the Rav contrasts the Rambam, who limits individual hashgacha to people, with the Ba'al Shem Tov, for whom it reaches every straw, and brings the Midrash of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and the bird. He adds the Gemara's story of a Tanna and the young lions and explains that even a predator's prey is timed by Heaven.

title.en: Stories of provision at the right moment

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov's thirsty disciple, who was given water by a man carrying it from a distant well for a madman poritz, and of a tzaddik who slapped his son for claiming hunger and then found a coin on the window. He concludes that Hashem shows His providence to whoever has simple emunah.

title.en: 'Poseach es yadecha': davening for parnassa

summary.en: The Rav explains that Ashrei is said three times a day because of 'Poseach es yadecha', and tells of the Strelisker, whose chassidim did not want parnassa, and of the Ruzhiner, who had them write it in their kvitlach. Bringing the Rambam, the Ramban and the Maharal, he explains that tefilah is an exercise in emunah and that asking for parnassa places one under Hashem's hashgacha.

title.en: Famine and plague; justice and mercy

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Taanis that when there was both plague and famine one should pray for food, since whoever is given sustenance is given life, hinted in 'umasbia lechol chai'. On 'Tzaddik Hashem bechol derachav' he explains that mercy can sweeten a decree of strict justice, and raises the Gemara's contradiction whether man is judged on Rosh Hashanah or every day.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov and the water carrier

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov showed a disciple a water carrier who one day complained bitterly and the next day thanked Hashem for his health and bread. The Ba'al Shem Tov explained that the decree is set on Rosh Hashanah but the measure of mercy is judged daily, which the Rav reads into 'tzaddik' and 'chasid'.

title.en: 'Karov Hashem': no tefilah is lost

summary.en: On 'Karov Hashem lechol kor'av' the Rav brings Rav Hirsch on calling in truth and the principle from the sefarim that every tefilah is answered, if not now then stored in a person's heavenly account. He brings the Yetev Lev that Avraham's tefilah for Sodom was kept for later generations, and the barren women remembered together with Sarah.

catalogTitle: “מבשרי אחזה אלקי” - Seeing Hashem Through the Wonders of the Human Body

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows how the eye, heart, lungs, digestion, brain and speech, each a wonder and all dependent on one another, testify that a person can see the Creator from his own body.

abstract.en: The Rav returns to the Chovos HaLevavos's mashal of ink spilled into a poem: nobody would accept it, yet people claim the world made itself. Even if they say no one can be certain, a doubt of one in a hundred would stop anyone from taking a pill from a tainted batch, as the Tylenol scare showed; their denial is rationalization driven by temptation. All of creation proclaims a Creator. He then explains that the point of studying the body is not to list its wonders, which would never end, but to train the mind to see Hashem, as the generation born in the desert marveled at bread growing from the ground. He goes through the eye, the heart, the lungs and the digestive system, stressing that each works automatically and that all depend on each other, then the brain and speech. Every organ has a purpose, so claiming it all happened by itself is a wild imagination that serves only the wish to do as one pleases.

en: Those who deny a Creator do not act this way about real dangers: a one-in-a-hundred doubt keeps anyone from a possibly poisoned bottle, so their denial is rationalization born of temptation.
The purpose of looking at the body is not to list its wonders but to train the mind, which takes everything for granted, to see Hashem everywhere.
The eye is a camera finer than any made, with automatic cleaning, protection and light adjustment.
The eye depends on the heart, the heart on the lungs, and all on the digestive system; each is a wonder and their working together is a further wonder.
Every part of the body has a purpose, so saying it all happened by itself is a wild imagination that serves the wish to do as one pleases.

summary.en: The Rav recalls the Chovos HaLevavos's mashal of spilled ink forming a poem, and uses the Tylenol poisoning scare to show that nobody takes a one-in-a-hundred risk; denying a Creator is rationalization driven by temptation, while all of creation proclaims there is a Creator.

title.en: Training the mind to see; the eye

summary.en: The Rav explains that looking at the body is meant to train the mind to see Hashem, like the generation born in the desert who marveled at bread growing from the ground. He then describes the eye: a camera finer than any made, with automatic tears, eyelashes, reflexes, pupil adjustment and two eyes for depth.

title.en: The eye needs the heart and lungs

summary.en: The Rav shows that the eye depends on blood for food and for removing wastes, which leads to the heart, a boneless piece of flesh that pumps for decades and speeds up by itself when a person runs. The heart in turn needs the lungs for oxygen, which also adjust their pace automatically.

title.en: The digestive system and interdependence

summary.en: The Rav describes the teeth, the tongue and its taste buds, the many colors and tastes Hashem gave food, swallowing and the stomach's acids, and asks why the stomach does not digest itself. He concludes that heart, lungs and digestion are each a wonder and all interdependent.

title.en: Brain, speech, and 'from my flesh'

summary.en: The Rav describes the brain cells that are never replaced so that memory endures, and the wonder of speech, applying 'from my flesh I see G-d' to a person's own body. He notes that medicine keeps finding a purpose for every organ, calls the denial rationalization, and closes that the aim is to train the mind to see Hashem in all of creation.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the closing verses of Ashrei and the opening of Halleluyah, Hallei Nafshi: how prayer opens Hashem's chesed beyond strict justice, how a tzaddik's praise awakens all of creation, and how a tzaddik praises Hashem with his very life.

abstract.en: The Rav distinguishes Hashem's general providence, which feeds every creature according to its desire, from His particular providence, which is just in all His ways yet can be changed through prayer, since He is also kind in all His deeds. He brings the Midrash of the treasure of free gifts, opened at special times, places and through tzaddikim. On 'Hashem is close to all who call Him,' he stresses calling in truth and that no prayer is lost. 'Hashem guards all who love Him' includes those attached to a tzaddik, while one who joins a rasha suffers with him. After Ashrei, David's praise as king awakens all flesh to praise. Halleluyah, Hallei Nafshi means David joins the praise he calls for. 'I will praise Hashem with my life': a tzaddik praises Him with his whole life, even his sleep and his very existence, and should trust only in Hashem.

en: Hashem's particular providence is just in all His ways, yet because He is also kind in all His deeds, prayer can annul a decree that was justly made.
The treasure of free gifts is the greatest of all, and there are special times, places and tzaddikim through which it opens.
Every prayer said sincerely is accepted; when its answer is not seen, Hashem credits it to the person's account for later or for his children.
Those who are attached to a tzaddik are guarded together with him, and one who joins a rasha is caught up in the rasha's punishment.
A tzaddik's praise of Hashem awakens the whole creation to praise Him, each tzaddik according to his sphere of influence, and David as king awakened all of Klal Yisrael.
In 'Halleluyah, Hallei Nafshi' David first calls on others to praise and then says that his own soul praises too, since one cannot tell others to do what he does not do himself.
A tzaddik praises Hashem with his life, through everything he does, while a rasha brings honor to Heaven only through his downfall.

title.en: General and particular providence

summary.en: The Rav explains 'You open Your hand' as the general providence that gives every creature what it desires, with examples of the ox, the flamingo and the cat. He then explains 'righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds' as the particular providence: a just decree that prayer can still annul.

title.en: The treasure of free gifts and times of favor

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash in which Moshe Rabbeinu was shown the treasure of free gifts, the greatest of all. He lists times, places and tzaddikim through which this treasure opens, and brings the Gemara in Berachos that Hashem grants even one who is not worthy.

title.en: Calling in truth; no prayer is lost

summary.en: On 'Hashem is close to all who call Him in truth' the Rav explains that prayer must be said with the mind on the words, bringing the Chovos HaLevavos' parable of the king, and that every sincere prayer is accepted even when no answer is seen. He then turns to 'He guards all who love Him' and the Gemara's teaching that the word 'es' includes what is secondary.

title.en: Joined to a tzaddik, joined to a rasha

summary.en: Following the Yismach Moshe, the Rav explains that 'es kol ohavav' includes those attached to a tzaddik, and 'all the wicked He will destroy' includes those who join a rasha. He brings the king of Yehudah who was punished for joining a rasha, and Avraham, to whom Hashem spoke only after Lot left him.

title.en: A tzaddik's praise awakens all flesh

summary.en: On 'My mouth will speak Hashem's praise, and all flesh will bless,' the Rav explains that a tzaddik's praise awakens all of creation, each tzaddik according to his sphere of influence, revealed or hidden. He brings the Gemara that King David ruled on questions and then asked Mefiboshes, and explains that David ruled himself because his word brought purity to all of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: After Ashrei, the urge to keep praising

summary.en: The Rav explains that when David finished Ashrei he was seized with longing to keep praising, and so began Halleluyah. He tells of a fiery Stoliner chassid who would say Pesukei DeZimra again with a second minyan, and of Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach, who would not ask others to give tzedakah without giving himself.

title.en: Praising with one's life, not one's downfall

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'Halleluyah' calls on others, and 'Hallei nafshi' says that David praises too; 'with my life' means putting one's whole vitality into prayer. He brings the verse that Hashem made everything for His sake, even the rasha for the day of evil, and explains that a rasha honors Heaven through his downfall, while David praises with his life.

title.en: A tzaddik is a tzaddik even in his sleep

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Chiddushei HaRim and Rav Yitzchak of Vorka watched Rav Yechezkel of Kuzmir sleep, and concludes that a Rebbe is a Rebbe even asleep. He explains 'with my being' as praising even through the secondary parts of life, and 'with my life' as thanks for life itself, telling of Rav Zusha dancing because he was hungry.

title.en: Do not trust in benefactors

summary.en: On 'Do not trust in benefactors' the Rav explains that only Hashem can truly help. He tells how the Chiddushei HaRim and the Vorker Rebbe considered asking Moses Montefiore to annul a Polish decree on the chadarim, and how the Chiddushei HaRim explained that one cannot rely on a person for whom the matter is not a salvation.

oneLiner.en: Going through the chapter of Tehillim 'Al tivtechu vindivim', the Rav explains that a Jew's hope rests only on Hashem, who measures every person's share of help and suffering, and that even when people help him they are only Hashem's messengers.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with 'Al tivtechu vindivim': the great donors cannot be relied on, since a man can change his mind or leave the world. Yaakov Avinu is the model of bitachon; the Midrash contrasts his empty-handed journey to Charan with Eliezer's camels, and he said 'my help is from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth'. Even when donors help, they are only messengers. Reading 'sivro' as 'shivro', the Rav explains that every person's measure of suffering is fixed, so one who pours his toil into Torah and avodas Hashem is spared suffering elsewhere. He goes on through the chapter: helpers and enemies are Hashem's instruments; Hashem keeps faith across generations and gilgulim, frees trapped sparks of holiness in their time, and watches over the orphan and widow. Bitachon is drawn from Torah, tzaddikim, and the 'Tziyon' of every generation, such as Shabbos. He closes on 'Ki tov zamrah Elokeinu': Dovid HaMelech sings even under midas hadin.

en: The Rav explains that one cannot rely on the donors, because a man may change his mind or leave the world, and with him his plans are lost.
Even when people do help, the one whose hope is on Hashem sees them only as a messenger; if they refuse, Hashem has another messenger.
Every person must go through suffering in this world, and how much is decreed in Heaven; nachas in one area means less in another, and suffering in one area spares another.
The Rav says one should put his exertion into avodas Hashem, toiling over a Tosafos or a blatt Gemara, and thereby be spared suffering in health and in nachas from children.
Hashem's reckoning is true over many generations: a loss or an unexpected ruling may settle an account from an earlier gilgul.
Bitachon is acquired by going to the Torah and to tzaddikim and by drawing from the 'Tziyon' of each generation, in place, in soul or in time, such as Shabbos.
'Ki tov zamrah Elokeinu' teaches that Dovid HaMelech sings to Hashem even when He acts with midas hadin, since everything Hashem does is for his good.

candidateTopics: measured suffering and toil in Torah
Tziyon in place, soul and time
Shabbos as a source of bitachon

title.en: Do not rely on the donors

summary.en: The Rav observes that the largest tzedakah comes from ordinary Jews of the batei midrash, not from the rich, and reads 'al tivtechu vindivim': a man can promise, then change his mind or leave the world, and his plans are lost with him.

title.en: Yaakov, the pillar of bitachon

summary.en: On 'ashrei she'Kel Yaakov b'ezro', the Rav brings the Midrash that Yaakov went to Charan with nothing, unlike Eliezer's camels, and said 'my help is from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth'. One whose hope is on Hashem sees even helping donors as mere messengers.

title.en: Every person's measure of suffering

summary.en: Bringing a reading of 'sivro' as 'shivro', the Rav explains that each person must go through a fixed measure of suffering and nachas. He tells of a man who lost a gold watch after having nachas from new curtains, and explains the custom of saying 'kaparah' over a broken glass.

title.en: Breaking oneself for Hashem

summary.en: Every person comes into the world to be broken, so the Rav says one should put his toil into Torah and avodas Hashem and be spared suffering in health and children. He asks why not everyone does so and answers that they lack bitachon; one whose breaking is 'al Hashem Elokav' shows true hope.

title.en: Helpers, enemies and Hashem's true reckoning

summary.en: On 'Hashem li b'ozrai', the Rav says one must thank those who help yet see Hashem behind them, and see an enemy too as Hashem's instrument, as Dovid did with Shimi ben Gera. On 'shomer emes l'olam' he explains, with Rashi, that Hashem's reckoning spans generations and gilgulim, illustrated by a din Torah before Reb Yitzchak Hamburger.

title.en: Hashem frees what is bound, in its time

summary.en: On 'Hashem matir asurim', the Rav explains that Hashem arranges ways, such as bitul b'rov, for a trapped spark of holiness to become permitted. A person may not force such a release himself, just as Klal Yisrael was sworn to wait for the geulah and not take it by force.

title.en: The blind, the bent, the orphan and the widow

summary.en: The Rav goes through 'pokeach ivrim', 'zokef kefufim', 'ohev tzaddikim' and 'yasom v'almanah ye'oded': those without worldly wisdom, those bent under burdens and the forsaken are not lost, for Hashem watches over them. He brings a letter of Reb Yonasan to his widowed sister that most orphans grow up successful, while the planned paths of the wicked are overturned.

title.en: Where bitachon is drawn from: Tziyon

summary.en: The Rav sums up the chapter's theme as bitachon and asks where it is acquired: from the Torah, from tzaddikim and their stories, and from 'Tziyon', which today exists in soul and in time, such as Shabbos. He tells the Gemara's story of Nakdimon ben Gurion to show that Hashem's kingship of 'yimloch Hashem l'olam' is present in every generation.

title.en: Singing to Hashem even in midas hadin

summary.en: Moving to 'Ki tov zamrah Elokeinu', the Rav explains that after Ashrei Dovid HaMelech could not stop praising. He contrasts mockers of long, loud davening with their own shouting at ball games, and explains that Dovid sings even under midas hadin, as in 'tzarah v'yagon emtza uvshem Hashem ekra'.

oneLiner.en: On the words 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes', the Rav teaches that every Jew is Hashem's messenger, and that the summer travels of Tammuz and Av, if made with awareness of the shlichus, gather sparks of holiness and build Yerushalayim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Sanzer Rav's teaching that every Jewish avodah builds the Beis Hamikdash, so that today only small things are missing, and with Dovid Hamelech's answer for why the building takes so long: Hashem is gathering the dispersed of Israel. Turning to Parshas Shelach, he brings the Chasam Sofer on the sending of the meraglim and develops the idea of shlichus: a sofer is holy only as Hashem's messenger, and every person is sent into the world on a mission, as the Sfas Emes says. A parable of a man who went to a land of diamonds and came back with spoiled tallow shows how people forget their mission. The summer travels, beginning with the forty days of the meraglim, are meant to repair their journey; the Ba'al Shem Tov teaches that Hashem sends each person where sparks await him. Galus itself serves this purpose. Tammuz and Av, the months of the eyes, call for guarding the eyes. He closes with a blessing for a healthy summer.

en: Every mitzvah and avodah of Jews builds the Beis Hamikdash; earlier generations built its great parts, and our small generation completes it with small things.
The building of Yerushalayim waits because Hashem first gathers the dispersed of Israel, as Dovid Hamelech says 'nidchei Yisrael yechanes'.
Every Jew doing a mitzvah, and every person who comes into the world, is a messenger of the Ribono shel Olam, and the holiness of his deed comes from the Sender.
The summer travels that begin with the forty days of the meraglim are meant to repair the meraglim's failed journey, but only if one remembers that he travels as Hashem's messenger.
Hashem sends each Jew to particular places, and Israel into galus, so that each soul can rectify the sparks of holiness that belong to it.
Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, so guarding the eyes in these months repairs the damage of the meraglim's seeing and prepares the rebuilding of Tziyon.

title.en: The Beis Hamikdash built from small deeds

summary.en: The Rav opens with Boneh Yerushalayim and tells how the Sanzer Rav said every avodah builds the Beis Hamikdash and only the paroches was missing. If so, today only small things remain, and he asks why the building takes so long, answering from 'nidchei Yisrael yechanes'.

title.en: The meraglim and the idea of shlichus

summary.en: On Parshas Shelach the Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that both Hashem's command and the people's request stood behind the sending of the meraglim. He explains that the sender's power rests in the messenger: a sofer writes holiness only as Hashem's shliach, Yehoshua's spies succeeded because they went as shluchim, and the Sfas Emes says every person is Hashem's messenger.

title.en: The parable of the land of diamonds

summary.en: The Rav tells a parable brought by a talmid of the Chasam Sofer: a poor man travels to a dark land whose streets are full of diamonds, but there candles are precious, so he forgets his purpose, fills his bags with tallow, and comes home with spoiled goods and only a few small diamonds.

title.en: The soul's forgotten mission

summary.en: The Rav explains the parable: the soul is sent down to collect the diamonds of Torah and mitzvos but fills its bags with worldly things. He describes people running after money, and explains that the angel who fought Yaakov would not reveal his name because angels are named for their mission, and the yetzer hara wants people to forget theirs.

title.en: Summer travel and the forty days of the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav notes that the meraglim set out on erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, and that the same season is when people go traveling. The purpose is to repair the meraglim's journey and turn Tisha B'Av into a festival, and the parsha of tzitzis that follows reminds a person, like a string tied on a finger, of his mission.

title.en: Sent to sparks that wait for us

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on 'Me'Hashem mitz'adei gever konanu': a Jew who travels to Chicago on business is really sent to a Jew of his soul-root or to fruit holding his sparks. A tree in the country has waited thousands of years for a Jew to learn under it; vacations, rest and eating are meant to give strength to serve Hashem.

title.en: Galus to gather the sparks

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yesod HaAvodah that one should always say 'it was not you who sent me here but G-d', and explains that every small act builds the Beis Hamikdash. Since Adam's sin scattered sparks across the world, Jews are sent to every land; he brings the Gemara and the Chasam Sofer on why galus is needed, and the Chasam Sofer on Rus.

title.en: Tammuz and Av, the months of the eyes

summary.en: Returning to Boneh Yerushalayim, the Rav explains that Jews must be in galus to gather the sparks, and that Tammuz and Av are especially suited to building the Beis Hamikdash and will become festivals. Hidden good lies in these months like pearls on the sea floor; following the Arizal they are the two eyes, so they bring the greatest tests of the eyes.

title.en: Guarding the eyes and repairing the nesi'im

summary.en: The Rav says guarding the eyes in the street is a precious avodah to rejoice in, repairing the eyes of these months toward seeing Hashem's return to Tziyon. He shows that the nesi'im of Reuven and Shimon, linked to Tammuz and Av, failed in Korach's dispute and with Zimri, and concludes that Jews travel to gather the sparks that complete Yerushalayim.

title.en: Blessing for a healthy summer

summary.en: The Rav blesses the listeners with a healthy, successful summer in which they fulfil their shlichus, and explains that a Jew must eat and sleep enough to be healthy so he can learn and daven. He begins a story of a chassid of the Tzemach Tzedek who davened at length, and the recording ends mid-story.

catalogTitle: Hashem Maintains a Balanced World with Breathtaking Precision

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that people who reject emunah are hiding from what they know, and that the precise balance of the world, from the oxygen in the air to ice floating on water, shows that Hashem maintains His world.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a letter printed in a newspaper after the Six-Day War, in which a woman asked the editor to stop writing about the miracles because they gave her a guilty conscience about driving to the beach on Shabbos. People, he says, bury their heads in the sand so that emunah will not hinder their desires. He illustrates this with a story the Telzer Rosh Yeshiva, Rav Bloch, wrote in his sefer: a ceiling that kept falling until boards soaked with a suicide's blood were buried, after which one boy stopped coming to the club so as not to see evidence of G-d. The Rav then dismisses fears that the world will be ruined, comparing them to Rashi's account of the Dor Haflagah, and shows Hashem's balance in nature: 21% oxygen, the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide, worms and birds, blood clotting, and water, which expands near freezing so that ice floats and fish survive. He ends noting that Jews too have their own pattern of behavior.

en: People do not truly disbelieve; they hide their belief because emunah would hinder their pursuit of desires.
The world cannot be ruined by human progress, because Hashem who made the world controls and maintains it, as a household with a master is in order.
The air always holds 21% oxygen, the exact amount that lets people breathe without the world catching fire, and the carbon dioxide people and animals breathe out feeds the plants.
Nature is balanced throughout: worms soften the earth for plants, birds keep the worms in check, and birds of prey keep the birds in check.
Blood clots only on contact with air, sealing a wound without blocking the veins, a built-in repair system that shows Hashem's wisdom.
Water, unlike other elements, expands as it nears freezing, so ice floats and fish and plants survive beneath it.
