title.en: The letter asking to stop writing about miracles

summary.en: The Rav describes the miracles of the Six-Day War and a letter to the editor from a woman in Tel Aviv who asked the paper to stop reporting them because they made her feel guilty about going to the beach on Shabbos. He says this shows how people bury their heads in the sand so emunah will not hinder their desires.

title.en: The ceiling that kept falling in the club

summary.en: The Rav tells a story the Telzer Rosh Yeshiva, Rav Bloch, wrote in his sefer: in a club of boys who had left Yiddishkeit, the ceiling kept falling until boards soaked with the blood of a boy who took his life were buried as the Shulchan Aruch requires. One boy then stopped coming so he would not see evidence of G-d, which shows that people hide their belief rather than lack it.

title.en: The balance of the air and of nature

summary.en: The Rav calls fears that pollution and deforestation will ruin the world nonsense, compares them to the Dor Haflagah's fear that the sky would collapse, as Rashi brings, and says Hashem maintains His world. He shows the balance of 21% oxygen, the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between people and plants, and the chain of worms, birds and birds of prey.

title.en: Blood clotting and expansion by heat

summary.en: The Rav explains that blood clots only on contact with air, sealing wounds without causing strokes or heart attacks, and notes hemophiliacs who lack this. He then introduces the law that every element expands when heated, using the gaps between railroad tracks.

title.en: Why ice floats

summary.en: After the thermometer, the Rav shows that water alone expands again as it nears freezing, so ice is lighter than water and floats, keeping fish and plants alive beneath it. He closes saying that Jews also have their own pattern of behavior, to be discussed the next week.

oneLiner.en: On the words 'Hallelukah ki tov zamrah', the Rav explains that song belongs to the 'eighth' level above nature, which will be revealed when Moshiach builds Yerushalayim and gathers in every last scattered Jew, each one precious to Hashem like a named star.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tehillim 147 as a continuation of 'Yimloch Hashem l'olam': in the days of Moshiach the whole world will know that it is good to sing to Hashem. He brings the Berditchever Rav's saying that a chazan is a fool, since the gates of song stand beside the gates of teshuvah, and stresses how great zimrah was in the Beis Hamikdash. He then builds the idea of the number eight, which is above the seven of nature: Shavuos after the sefirah, Chanukah, milah, the eight-stringed kinor of Moshiach, Cheshvan and the third Beis Hamikdash, teshuvah, and the musical octave in which the eighth note is the first again. Moshiach will add a new note. On 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' he links the Rambam's signs of Moshiach, Yerushalayim as the heart of the world, and the Jews as the heart of history. Every Jew is a letter in the Torah; the broken last letters will join the first. The galus lasts long because Hashem waits for every Jew, as He names every star, and His reckoning is above number.

en: The Rav reads 'Hallelukah ki tov zamrah' as a continuation of 'Yimloch Hashem l'olam': in the days of Moshiach the world will recognize that singing to Hashem is good.
Eight stands for what is above the seven of nature: Chanukah, milah, Shavuos, teshuvah and the third Beis Hamikdash all belong to it.
In music the eighth note of the octave is the first again, which the Rav connects to teshuvah, a return to the root; Moshiach will bring a new, eighth note.
The two halves of 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' match the Rambam's two signs of Moshiach: building the Beis Hamikdash and gathering the exiles.
Yerushalayim is the heart of the world, and the Jewish people are the heart of all that happens in history.
The galus lasts so long because Hashem wants every scattered Jew to reach his tikkun, so that no Jew is left out.
Like the stars, which Hashem counts and calls each by name, every Jew is an individual with a name before Hashem, not a number.

title.en: Hallelukah ki tov zamrah and the power of song

summary.en: The Rav opens the new chapter as a continuation of 'Yimloch Hashem l'olam', about the days of Moshiach. He brings the Berditchever Rav's saying that a chazan is a fool, since the gates of song are beside the gates of teshuvah, and describes zimrah in the Beis Hamikdash and its revival by the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov.

title.en: Eight: above the seven of nature

summary.en: The Rav explains that seven stands for the middos and the world of nature, and eight for what is above it. He brings Shavuos after the sefirah, the Maharal on Chanukah, milah on the eighth day, the Gemara in Arachin on the kinor of eight strings in the days of Moshiach, the Bnei Yissaschar on Cheshvan and the third Beis Hamikdash, and teshuvah, which preceded the world.

title.en: The octave, teshuvah and the new note of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav says much wisdom of music came from the Jews, and shows that in the octave the eighth note is the first again. This explains the Berditchever's words, and why in the days of Moshiach, the 'eighth', a new note will be added and it will be good to sing to Hashem.

title.en: Boneh Yerushalayim and the signs of Moshiach

summary.en: On 'Boneh Yerushalayim Hashem, nidchei Yisrael yechanes' the Rav brings the Rambam's two signs of Moshiach, building the Beis Hamikdash and gathering the exiles, and calls this the return of yovel and of teshuvah. He then begins to explain that Yerushalayim is the heart of the world.

title.en: Yerushalayim and the Jews: the heart of the world

summary.en: The Rav shows from the Zohar, the Kuzari and history that everything revolves around Eretz Yisrael and Yerushalayim, from the news to the wars and the world's religions, and that the turning point against Rommel came at its border. Everything in the world happens for the sake of the Jews, as the Nazi leader's obsession with killing the Jews of Hungary at the cost of the war shows.

title.en: From beis to lamed: the broken heart made whole

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew is a letter in the Torah: the great souls are the beis of Bereishis and the last generations are the last letters, with the broken lamed. When the Torah is read as a circle, as on Simchas Torah, the lamed meets the beis; so Moshiach, the soul of Moshe, will join the broken Jews to the first, and this is 'Harofei lishvurei lev'.

title.en: Why the galus lasts so long

summary.en: Returning to the passuk, the Rav says that then one will sing even about the middas hadin of the galus. He asks why the galus lasts so long and answers that Hashem waits for every scattered Jew to reach his tikkun, and tells of a tzaddik who would not bring Moshiach at the cost of losing such Jews.

title.en: Moneh mispar lakochavim: a name, not a number

summary.en: The Rav compares a Jew who seems to be nothing to a newly found star many times larger than the earth. On 'Moneh mispar lakochavim, lechulam shemos yikra' he explains the difference between a number and a name, with the cattle herd, children, the Nazis' tattooed numbers and the counting 'b'mispar shemos', and says every creation and every Jew has a function no other can fill.

title.en: Lisvunaso ein mispar: Hashem's reckoning above number

summary.en: The Rav asks how a Jew who shows no Jewishness can hold up the geulah, and answers with 'Gadol Adoneinu… lisvunaso ein mispar': Hashem's understanding does not work with numbers. Tzion is above the laws of mathematics, as the Aron took up no space and the crowded Azarah had room for all, and so one must wait for 'Boneh Yerushalayim'.

oneLiner.en: Going through the psalm of Hallelukah ki tov zamrah, the Rav explains that Hashem counts and names every Jew like the stars, that every creature has its own mission, and that the hardships of exile are a preparation for the song of the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: Returning to the verse 'He counts the number of the stars, He calls them all by name', the Rav explains that every Jew, even the broken and forgotten, has a name, and a name is a mission. He digresses to Adam naming Chava after the curse, and tells how a Rebbe declined to name a child for its father. A name change for a sick person gives him a new mission. People who seem small and unlucky are like the stars, which only look small. From Gadol Adoneinu and me'oded anavim he teaches that every person contributes to the world. When Moshiach comes, a new song will reveal the purpose of exile, which is like clouds and rain that make things grow. Hashem feeds even the raven's young, and the ravens fed Eliyahu, a soul of the days of Moshiach. Hashem desires those who hope for Him, not the strength of horses. Even decrees in exile are softened, like snow that falls as wool.

en: Every Jew has a name and not a number, and his name is his particular mission in the world.
People who seem insignificant are like the stars, which look small but are enormous, and every creature, down to a caterpillar, has a mission without which the world would not be complete.
When Moshiach comes a new song will be sung, because then it will be seen what the exile and the small, forgotten people accomplished.
The exile is like a dreary, rainy day whose clouds and rain prepare the growth of a spring that will come with the redemption.
Hashem desires not physical might but those who fear Him and hope for His kindness every day.
Even in exile Hashem softens harsh decrees, as snow comes down like wool and is scattered like dust.

title.en: A name is a mission; Adam names Chava

summary.en: The Rav returns to the verse about Hashem naming the stars: every Jew has a name, and a name is a mission, as the Arizal and Rashi show. In a digression he explains how Adam, instead of blaming Chava after the curses, named her 'mother of all life', and Hashem in turn clothed them.

title.en: Names, illness, and the unseen greatness of the small

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Chiddushei HaRim refused to choose a child's name for its father, explains that a name change can give a sick person a new mission, and compares people whose lives seem failed to the stars, which only look small. Every creature, even a caterpillar, is a needed part of the great machine of creation.

title.en: Gadol Adoneinu: encouragement for the humble

summary.en: From 'Great is our Lord, His understanding is beyond number' the Rav explains that every person does something good for the world, even the worst rasha who once did a mitzvah. 'Hashem encourages the humble' is a chizuk for small people, while the oppressors who build themselves on others are brought low.

title.en: The new song of Moshiach and the clouds of exile

summary.en: The Rav explains that these psalms speak of the coming of Moshiach, when a new song will be sung for everything not understood before. The exile, with its questions, is like a dark rainy day; 'He covers the heavens with clouds' to prepare the rain that makes the spring bloom.

title.en: Singing now; Hashem feeds the raven's young

summary.en: The Rav says Dovid HaMelech calls on a person to sing to Hashem already now, with the abilities he has. 'He gives the animal its bread, to the young ravens' shows that every creature counts: Hashem feeds the raven's chicks though the raven, which lacked mercy in the ark, abandons them. The ravens that fed Eliyahu show that in the days of Moshiach the raven will become merciful.

title.en: Not the strength of the horse, but those who hope

summary.en: On 'Not in the strength of the horse does He desire', the Rav contrasts the nations' pride in might, which he ties to the Greek culture of sport fought on Chanukah, with what Hashem wants. Hashem desires those who fear Him and hope every day for Moshiach, as the Rambam counts among the principles of faith.

title.en: Praise, Yerushalayim, and the swift redemption

summary.en: The Rav explains 'Praise Hashem, Yerushalayim' as addressed to the Jewish people even while the city lies in ruins, promising strengthened gates, peaceful borders and the finest wheat. To the question how to praise for a hope not yet fulfilled, he answers from 'He sends His word to the earth, swiftly runs His word': when the time comes, the redemption comes at once, as seen in the Megillah.

title.en: Snow like wool: the decree softened

summary.en: On 'He gives snow like wool', the Rav explains that Hashem gives the cold of exile according to the warmth a person has, and when Jews daven strongly a decree that cannot be undone is crushed to powder, like the mashal of the king who had the stone ground before it was thrown at his son. Snow is middas hadin, yet Hashem sweetens it with mercy, and Jews survive the exile.

oneLiner.en: Through the closing verses of Tehillim 147, the Rav shows how Hashem sweetens His din, how rain and snow are rooted in chesed and carry Torah, and how a Jew keeps the chok with simple emunah until he is granted to understand it.

abstract.en: The Rav continues with the verse 'He casts His ice like crumbs'. Nissan and the summer are a time of chesed, of warmth and expansion; Tishrei and the winter are din and contraction, and from the cold comes ice. Yet Hashem sweetens the din: the ice falls as flakes, and the snow is white, the color of chesed, like milk and the manna, food given without toil. Then 'He sends His word and melts them': snow is frozen water, and water is chesed. The rain carries blessing and, inwardly, Torah. The Rav brings the Zohar that Noach could have received the Torah and returned as Moshe, and explains Matan Torah as a 'mabul' of Torah. On 'His chukim and mishpatim to Yisrael' he describes the Akeidah: Avraham went with emunah shleimah without understanding, and only afterward understood. He closes with Tehillim 148 and man's role in leading all creation in praise.

en: The summer months from Nissan are a time of chesed, warmth and expansion, while the winter months from Tishrei are din, cold and contraction.
Hashem sweetens the din of winter: the ice comes down as flakes and the snow is white, the color of chesed, like milk and the manna, which are food given freely.
The root of snow is water, which is chesed; when Hashem melts it, the rain brings blessing, and the inner soul of rain is Torah.
At Matan Torah the heavens showed the sign of a mabul, but instead of a flood of water there came down a flood of Torah.
Avraham went to the Akeidah with emunah shleimah, without understanding how Hashem's promise about Yitzchak would be kept, and the test of emunah is to believe even with questions.
First comes the chok, kept without understanding, and afterward the mishpat, when Hashem grants understanding to those who keep the Torah.
Man, and the Jew in particular, holds the control of all creation, so that the angels' praise depends on the praise of the Jews.

title.en: Months of chesed and months of din

summary.en: Returning to 'He casts His ice like crumbs', the Rav explains that from Nissan begins a rule of chesed, shown in the straight order of the letters of 'aviv', while Tishrei is din, its letters in reverse. Summer is warmth and expansion, winter is cold and contraction, and from that din comes the ice.

title.en: Why the snow is white

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem sends the ice as flakes and answers that He sweetens the din with rachamim. The whiteness of the snow is chesed, like milk, the food of infants who are exempt from toiling for bread, and like the white manna of the generation of the desert; then a thaw gives people and animals relief.

title.en: The thaw, the rain and its soul

summary.en: On 'He sends His word and melts them', the Rav explains that the root of snow is water, which is chesed, held back in winter and released by Hashem's wind. Rain brings great blessing, as the Gemara in Taanis says, and since every physical thing has a soul, the soul of rain is Torah.

title.en: Noach, Moshe and a mabul of Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that the Torah could have been given through Noach, and that Noach's soul returned as Moshe, which explains the Gemara's hint of Moshe in 'beshagam' and why the flood is called 'the waters of Noach'. He then explains the nations' fear of a flood at Matan Torah: it was a flood of Torah, and the letter shin turns 'mabul' into 'b'shalom'.

title.en: The rainy season and 'maggid'

summary.en: The Rav says a rainy day brings down an influence of Torah, so the rainy season, when one asks for rain for blessing, is a time to merit Torah. He explains 'maggid' as drawing forth, like the gidim that carry blood to the limbs: through the rain Hashem channels His word to Yaakov.

title.en: The Akeidah: emunah without understanding

summary.en: The Rav describes the test of the Akeidah: Hashem had promised that the nation would come from Yitzchak, who had no children, and now commanded to offer him. Avraham did not understand, yet went with emunah shleimah, leaving the 'how' to Hashem; many failed this test in the Holocaust, and the Rav answers with the mashal of a tailor cutting silk.

title.en: First the chok, then the mishpat

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who keeps the mitzvos without understanding is afterward granted understanding, while one who demands reasons first is never shown the sweetness of Shabbos or of learning. This is 'His chukim and mishpatim to Yisrael': first a chok, then a mishpat, as Avraham understood the Akeidah only afterward; the nations do not know even the mishpatim.

title.en: Man leads creation in praise

summary.en: Beginning Tehillim 148, the Rav explains that man was given control over the upper and lower worlds, a control that passed to Avraham and the Jews, so that the angels praise only after the Jews do. Man is the living soul of creation, and David HaMelech calls on heaven and earth to sing together; 'shamayim' means the remote 'there', and 'meromim' a height beyond grasp.

catalogTitle: Recognizing Hashem Through the Wonders of the Torah

oneLiner.en: Turning from the wonders of creation to the wonders of the Torah, the Rav shows from its endless depth, the wisdom contained in it, its fulfilled promises and the survival of the Jewish people with their Torah that the Torah is from Heaven.

abstract.en: After earlier weeks on the wonders of creation, the Rav turns to the wonders of the Torah. A man-made work, a poem or a painting, is exhausted once understood, and a schoolboy discards each year's books; yet the same Chumash and the same Eilu Metziyos serve a child, a bochur and the greatest gedolim, each finding more depth, just as scientists never finish discovering nature. Everything is in the Torah: he tells how the Ramban showed his student Avner, who had become a heretic, his own name in Ha'azinu, and how the Chazon Ish guided surgeons and said everything is in the Torah. He then shows the Torah's promises fulfilled: the conquest by Yehoshua, the division of the land by lottery as Yaakov and Moshe foretold, the protection of property during aliyah l'regel, and above all the survival of the Jewish people and their Torah through a long exile while their oppressors vanished.

en: A man-made wisdom is exhausted once understood, but the same Chumash and Gemara reveal ever more depth to a child, a bochur and the greatest gedolim, which shows the Torah is Divine wisdom.
Like nature, which scientists never finish exploring because Hashem made it, the Torah is endless.
Everything is in the Torah: the Sages knew all the wisdoms, such as agriculture, astronomy and geometry, from the Torah, and the Rav saw this in his own time in the Chazon Ish.
The Torah's promises, written down before they happened, were fulfilled to the letter: Yehoshua's conquest, the division of the land by lottery, and the safety of property during aliyah l'regel.
The survival of the Jewish people in a long exile, while all their mighty oppressors disappeared, and the living Torah learning of today, are a wonder that shows the Torah is from Heaven.

title.en: From wonders of creation to wonders of Torah

summary.en: The Rav turns from the wonders of creation to the wonders of the Torah, which a deep learner sees show it is not man-made. He contrasts a poem or a painting, which yields nothing new on rereading, and a schoolboy who must replace his books every year.

title.en: The same Chumash and Eilu Metziyos, ever deeper

summary.en: A child in cheder keeps the same Chumash and later the same Eilu Metziyos as a bochur, an old man and the gedolim, each seeing more depth. The Rav compares this to nature, which scientists never finish discovering because Hashem made it.

title.en: The Ramban and Avner: everything is in Ha'azinu

summary.en: The Rav tells the story of the Ramban's student Avner, who became a heretic because he could not believe that everyone is alluded to in Ha'azinu, and how the Ramban showed him his name in the third letters of four words of a passuk there.

title.en: All wisdoms are in the Torah: the Chazon Ish

summary.en: Citing the Ramban's introduction to Chumash, the Rav explains that the Sages knew all the sciences from the Torah, and tells how the Chazon Ish guided surgeons in America and told an astonished surgeon that everything is in the Torah.

title.en: Promises of the Torah fulfilled

summary.en: The Rav shows the Torah's truth from promises written in advance that came true: the land promised to the Avos, the Zohar on the round earth, Yehoshua's conquest, the lottery that matched what Yaakov and Moshe told each shevet, and the safety of fields during the three pilgrimages.

title.en: The wonder of Jewish survival in exile

summary.en: Moshe foretold exile but promised the people would remain a nation; the Rav shows how Rome, Greece and the other oppressors vanished while the Jews survived, even Hitler, and calls this a greater wonder than the Exodus. He ends with the promise that the Torah will not be forgotten, seen in the multitudes learning today.

catalogTitle: הללוקה הללו את ה' מן השמים

oneLiner.en: Going through Tehillim 148 and the opening of 149, the Rav explains that all of creation sings to Hashem by doing His will, but the praise of man, who has free choice, is the greater one, and that in the days of Mashiach the honest Jews who praise Hashem now in disgrace will be honored.

abstract.en: The Rav explains Tehillim 148 verse by verse. David HaMelech, as the soul of Adam and the key of creation, commands the heavens, the angels, the sun and moon and the higher heavens to praise Hashem, because through the service of the tzaddik all of creation sings. Their song is simply doing Hashem's will, as in Perek Shirah, since they were created by His command and have no free choice. He then turns to the earth: the sea creatures, fire and hail, and the storm wind, which even as the harshest klipah does Hashem's word, so that every bullet has an address. Domem, tzomeach, chai and medaber, and even kings, are like puppets on strings. Men have free choice; the wicked who carry out a decree are punished because they volunteered. Therefore the praise of earth comes before heaven, and in the days of Mashiach the chassidim, now mocked, will be honored and a new song with an eighth note will be sung.

en: David HaMelech, as the soul of Adam and the key of creation, can command all of creation to praise Hashem, because the service of the tzaddik is what causes the whole creation to sing.
The song of every creation is the very fact that it does Hashem's will: a caterpillar climbing a tree or a flowing stream is singing its shirah.
The heavenly hosts have no free choice; they function by a fixed law, 'chok nasan velo ya'avor', while man in the lower world has free choice.
Even the most harmful forces, the storm wind and the kings of the earth, can do nothing except as Hashem commands; every bullet has an address.
Because men praise Hashem out of free choice, the earth is mentioned before the heavens in 'hodo al eretz veshamayim'.
In exile honest Jews are mocked and called crazy, but when Mashiach comes they will be honored, and a new song will be sung to Hashem.

title.en: David calls on the heavens to praise

summary.en: The Rav explains that David HaMelech, the soul of Adam and the key of creation, commands the heavens, the angels, the sun and moon and the higher heavens to praise Hashem. He brings the Rambam that the heavenly bodies have intellect and sing, and explains that it is the tzaddik's service that causes creation to sing.

title.en: The song of creation is doing His will

summary.en: On 'ki hu tzivah venivra'u' the Rav explains that the shirah of every creature, as in Perek Shirah, is that it does Hashem's will, from the sun Yehoshua stopped to a caterpillar and a stream. The heavenly hosts were set by a law they cannot transgress and have no free choice, unlike our world.

title.en: Praise from the earth and the storm wind

summary.en: David turns to the earth: the sea creatures, fire and hail, snow and the storm wind. The Rav explains the four klipos of Yechezkel's vision, of which the storm wind is the worst, and shows that even it does Hashem's word and can harm only with His permission, so that every bullet has an address.

title.en: Four levels of creation and the kings

summary.en: The Rav shows that the verses follow the four levels of domem, tzomeach, chai and medaber, ending with the kings, princes and judges of the earth, who are like puppets on strings in Hashem's hand. He then reads 'bachurim vegam besulos' with the Sefer Chassidim, illustrated with a story about strawberries with cream.

title.en: Free choice makes man's praise greater

summary.en: Men have free choice, yet Hashem's will is done regardless; the wicked who serve as His agents are punished because they volunteered, as the Rambam discusses about Pharaoh. Because men can choose not to praise, their praise shows that Hashem's name alone is exalted, and so earth comes before heaven in the verse.

title.en: The honor of Klal Yisrael in Mashiach's days

summary.en: On 'vayarem keren le'amo, tehilah lechol chasidav' the Rav explains that in the days of Mashiach it will be revealed that the Jews were always the center of creation and the conductors of its song. Today Jews are disgraced among the nations and the chassidim among the Jews, and this is what we pray for on Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Called crazy: the honest Jew in exile

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara on the time before Mashiach, that one who turns from evil is considered mad, the Lechovitcher's blessing to his chassidim that they be called crazy, and the story of a refugee in Detroit whose uncle called him crazy for not working on Shabbos. When Mashiach comes it will be clear who is really crazy.

title.en: A new song for the time of Mashiach

summary.en: On 'shiru laHashem shir chadash, tehilaso bikhal chasidim' the Rav brings the Midrash that the angels will say kadosh before the tzaddikim, so a new song will be needed for Hashem. He brings the Rambam and the Yerushalmi that simple Jews will then have perceptions greater than prophets, and describes the new song as music with an eighth note.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 149, the Rav explains the 'new song' of the time of Moshiach, when the joy of Hashem and of Klal Yisrael will be complete for the first time, the hard times of galus will be seen as kindness, and the chassidim will sing in perfect bitachon.

abstract.en: The Rav learns Tehillim 149 verse by verse. A new world order will need a new song, sung above all by the chassidim, as at the Simchas Beis HaSho'eivah. Though the world looks worse, it grows better each year; every Chanukah brings down a greater light, and the new grain is permitted only after Pesach, the festival of redemption. 'Yismach Yisrael b'osav' teaches that until Moshiach neither Hashem nor any person has had complete joy; Shlomo HaMelech alone, at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, a foretaste of Moshiach, fulfilled all his desires. At the end of days the tzaddikim will dance in a circle, and the drum of galus will be praised together with the harp. Yosef's suffering proved to be for his good. 'Yerannenu al mishkevosam' is bitachon, shown by Chizkiyahu and Yaakov Avinu, opposed by Pharaoh; Kislev is the month of bitachon.

en: In the time of Moshiach a new era will be revealed, and the present forms of song will not suffice; a new song on new instruments will be needed to praise Hashem for it.
Although the world appears to grow worse, it is in truth getting better each year, coming closer to its tikkun; every Shabbos and every Chanukah is greater than the one before.
Until Moshiach comes there has been no complete joy, neither for Hashem with His creation nor for any person, who never fully attains his aspirations.
When Moshiach comes, the blows of galus, like the beating of a drum, will be recognized as Hashem's kindness and praised together with the sweet sounds of the harp.
'Yerannenu al mishkevosam' describes bitachon: a person at peace with Hashem can sleep, while one who lacks something lies awake in fear.
Kislev is the month of bitachon; it is a time for a Jew to gird himself with trust in Hashem, as the Chashmonaim did.

title.en: A new song for a new world

summary.en: The Rav opens Tehillim 149 and explains that a new era will need new forms of song, sung chiefly by the chassidim, as at the Simchas Beis HaSho'eivah. He adds that the world, though it looks worse, grows better each year, and that every Chanukah brings down a new light.

title.en: Chanukah's light and the new grain

summary.en: The Rav shows that Chanukah's greatness was revealed only in later generations, being the light of Moshiach, and that each year the yomim tovim grow brighter. Through the sparks of holiness in bread he explains why the new grain is permitted only once Pesach, the festival of redemption, arrives.

title.en: Yismach Yisrael b'osav

summary.en: The Rav explains the plural 'osav' as a term of majesty, and brings that at every Jewish simcha the souls of the ancestors come down, with an episode from the Skverer Rebbe's wedding. From the Midrash on 'yismach' he concludes that neither Hashem nor Klal Yisrael has yet had complete joy; it will come with Moshiach.

title.en: Shlomo HaMelech's day of complete joy

summary.en: The Rav asks why no person ever fulfills all his ambitions, and answers that one cannot be better off than Hashem, whose joy in creation is not yet complete. The one exception was Shlomo HaMelech at the dedication of the Beis HaMikdash, the full moon fifteen generations from Avraham and a sample of Moshiach, which is why the Haftarah of Shemini Atzeres ends with his fulfilled desire.

title.en: The circle dance, the drum and the harp

summary.en: After noting the small meal of Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah, the Rav explains 'yehallelu shemo vemachol': with Moshiach the tzaddikim will dance in a circle, all equal, as the Gemara at the end of Taanis describes. He contrasts the drum's beating with the harp's sweetness, and says the blows of galus will then be praised as Hashem's kindness.

title.en: Ki rotzeh Hashem b'amo: Yosef appeased

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash linking 'vayritzuhu min habor' to 'ki rotzeh Hashem b'amo': when Yosef left prison he saw that all his suffering had been for his good. So too Hashem will appease His people, and 'yefaer anavim bishuah' means He will crown the downtrodden of galus with salvation.

title.en: Singing on their beds: bitachon and sleep

summary.en: On 'ya'lzu chasidim bechavod, yerannenu al mishkevosam' the Rav explains that the worried cannot sleep while one with bitachon sleeps in peace. He brings the Midrash on Chizkiyahu, who slept the night Sancheirev besieged Yerushalayim, and Yaakov Avinu, who laid the stones of the mizbe'ach around his head as protection and slept.

title.en: Pharaoh's sleep and Kislev, month of bitachon

summary.en: The Rav says emunah comes from Avraham and bitachon from Yaakov, and contrasts Pharaoh, who went to sleep on the night of the plague of the firstborn, which Hashem arranged to strengthen the bitachon of the Jews. He closes with Kislev, named for bitachon and linked to sleep in Sefer Yetzirah, as a time to serve Hashem with trust as the Chashmonaim did.

catalogTitle: “ולגדלתו אין חקר”- The Human Mind is not Capable of Understanding G-dliness

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why chakirah, philosophy, is a dangerous and unreliable path to emunah: the human mind is not the organ that grasps Hashem, while the neshamah, a part of G-d above, can feel Him unless aveiros insulate it.

abstract.en: After reviewing two approaches to emunah, inherited faith and seeing Hashem's wonders, the Rav turns to a third, chakirah or philosophy. He notes that yeshivos learn the Rambam's halachos but not his Moreh Nevuchim, and explains why: philosophy is mental acrobatics, and a sharper mind can always refute a proof. Jewish philosophy arose in Arab lands to keep Jews from Greek thought, but the Gedolei Yisrael rejected it, and the Rav tells how Rabbeinu Yonah, after Gemaras were burned in Paris, did teshuvah for his part in burning the Rambam's sefer. The mind, made of flesh, cannot grasp the Creator, as a watch cannot understand the watchmaker; the organ for that is the neshamah and nevuah, which aveiros insulate. Philosophy exposes a person to the kasha without the teretz. He closes with the Spanish expulsion, where simple Jews gave their lives while the philosophers converted.

en: Philosophy proves nothing, because any logical proof can be refuted by a sharper mind.
The Gedolei Yisrael of Ashkenaz never took to philosophy; it was a foreign import, while the Torah was received at Sinai.
The human mind, made of flesh, grasps only what is earthly and cannot understand Hashem, just as a watch cannot understand the watchmaker.
Hashem is perceived through a sixth sense, nevuah and ruach hakodesh, which every Jew has through his neshamah according to his level.
Aveiros insulate the neshamah and deaden its feeling, and teshuvah restores it.
Philosophy is dangerous because a person may grasp the kasha without the teretz, and even while weighing both sides he is for that moment not believing.

summary.en: The Rav reviews the two earlier approaches to emunah and introduces a third, chakirah. He notes that yeshivos learn the Rambam's halachos but not his Moreh Nevuchim, and explains that philosophy is mental acrobatics that a sharper mind can always refute, so it proves nothing.

title.en: Gedolei Yisrael and Rabbeinu Yonah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Jewish philosophy was written in Arab lands to shield Jews from Greek philosophy, while the Gedolei Yisrael rejected it as a human product. He tells how Rabbeinu Yonah, after Gemaras were burned in Paris, did teshuvah for his role in burning the Rambam's sefer and wrote Shaarei Teshuvah.

title.en: The mind is not the organ for G-dliness

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem cannot be proven by logic because He is above the mind, which is made of flesh and understands only the earthly. A watch cannot understand its watchmaker, and claiming to understand Hashem with the mind is like listening to a painting or watching a symphony.

title.en: The neshamah's sixth sense and aveiros

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sixth sense for knowing Hashem is ruach hakodesh and nevuah, which every Jew has through his neshamah. Aveiros wrap the neshamah like insulation on a wire or Novocaine in the gums, and teshuvah brings the feeling back.

title.en: A guide for the perplexed, and the kasha without the teretz

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the Ramchal's Mesillas Yesharim with the Rambam's Moreh Nevuchim, written for those who are lost and cannot yet be lit by Torah. He explains that the Gedolim discouraged philosophy because one may hear the kasha without the teretz, and shows from Ein K'Elokeinu that we say the answer before the question.

title.en: The expulsion from Spain

summary.en: The Rav tells from the Or HaChaim of Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz that at the expulsion from Spain, on Tisha B'Av, simple Jews and women gave their lives for emunah, while those steeped in philosophy converted. He concludes that philosophy is a dangerous path to emunah and should be rejected, and promises a fourth approach next time.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the closing verses of Tehillim 149 and the whole of Tehillim 150, showing how every voice, every instrument and finally the silent neshama join in the praise of Hashem that will be complete when Moshiach comes.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tehillim 149: the chassidim carry the praises of Hashem in their throat as a double-edged sword, praising Him even before the salvation comes. The revenge on the nations at the end of days will be the truth itself, when they see that the whole exile was for the good of the Jews, just as Yosef's brothers discovered that the 'ruler of the land' was their brother. From the hadar of the chassidim he turns to the eighth king, Hadar, as a hint to the eighth world of Moshiach. He then shows how Tehillim is framed by Tehilla leDavid and the closing Halleluka chapters, and explains Tehillim 150 verse by verse: praise as union with Hashem, praise for gevurah as for chesed, the shofar and the sweet instruments, the drum that keeps the rhythm, and finally the neshama, the silent instrument that gives life to all the songs.

en: The praises of Hashem in the mouth of the chassidim are their double-edged sword, with which they overcome every obstacle and enemy.

The vengeance on the nations in the days of Moshiach will be the revealed truth that the entire exile was for the good of the Jews, as Yosef's brothers discovered the 'harsh ruler' was their loving brother.
The eighth king of Edom, Hadar, alludes to the 'eighth world' of Moshiach, which is above the seven days of creation and has no death.
Halleluka is one word because a Jew who praises Hashem should cleave to Him until he is nullified like a candle before a torch.
One praises Hashem for His gevurah and judgment just as for His chesed.
After all the instruments comes the neshama, the silent instrument that is not heard yet gives the breath of life to all the songs of praise.

title.en: Praise as a double-edged sword

summary.en: The Rav explains 'romemos Kel bigronam' as the chassidim praising Hashem even before their salvation, and calls this praise the double-edged sword that defeats every enemy. He then reads 'la'asos nekama bagoyim' as the revenge of the truth revealed at the end of days.

title.en: Yosef and his brothers: the exile turned around

summary.en: The Rav compares the end of exile to Yosef revealing himself: the brothers thought the ruler of Egypt was their enemy, and with the words 'ani Yosef' everything turned around. So the nations will see that the whole exile was for Israel's good, and that truth will be their shame and their punishment, 'mishpat kasuv' and 'hadar' for the chassidim.

title.en: The eighth king, Hadar, and the eighth world

summary.en: The Rav brings the parsha of the kings of Edom at the end of Vayishlach: seven kings reigned and died, but of the eighth, Hadar, no death is written. Hadar hints at the eighth world of Moshiach; he connects it to the esrog of Sukkos and Shemini Atzeres, to the eighth day of Chanukah and to Pharaoh's interpreters who could reach only seven.

title.en: Tehillim's close and the one word Halleluka

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tehilla leDavid is the crown of Tehillim, after which David asks all flesh to join his praise, opening the Halleluka chapters. He then explains that Halleluka is one word because the one who praises must become one with Hashem, nullified like a candle before a torch.

title.en: Praise below and above; gevurah and gedulah

summary.en: The Rav explains that praise in the Beis Hamikdash and the shul gives the angels the power to praise in heaven. He explains why chesed is called gedulah (it spreads outward) and gevurah is contraction, and says one praises Hashem for His judgment just as for His kindness.

title.en: The instruments of praise

summary.en: The Rav explains the instruments of Tehillim 150: the shofar that brings fear, the sweet nevel and kinor, the drum that keeps the rhythm of the dance, and the cymbals. Even the noise of the drum is part of the symphony of Hashem's guidance of the world, and in the days of Moshiach every Jewish soul will reach its tikkun and join this praise.

title.en: David signs his name: Adam, David, Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'kol haneshama' is David's signature at the end of Tehillim: Adam, who included all souls, came again as David and will come as Moshiach. He then returns to the frame: after Tehilla leDavid David asks everyone to join, and 'Halleluka ki tov zamra' tells how sweet praise is, as anyone who has had a good davening knows.

title.en: From all creation to a new song to the neshama

summary.en: The Rav traces the last chapters: in 148 all creation, even the stormy wind of the klipah, praises; in 149 every creature should add a new song, quality rather than quantity; in 150 come all the instruments. Last comes the neshama, the inaudible instrument that gives life to all the praise, and he says one must praise with the whole soul and with hislahavus.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות אל ה' בצרתה לי

oneLiner.en: Learning the first two Shir Hamaalos (Tehillim 120 and 121), the Rav explains that the galus is a climb up to Yerushalayim, that a Jew must pray for the Shechinah's pain and guard his mouth from every trace of falsehood, and that when no help remains in this world, help comes from above nature.

abstract.en: Having finished Pesukei d'Zimra, the Rav turns to the fifteen Shir Hamaalos, which the Gemara links to David HaMelech's digging of the foundations of the mizbe'ach and to the fifteen steps on which the Levi'im sang; they form an ascent from galus to the Beis HaMikdash. On 'el Hashem batzarasa li' he explains that the troubles of galus are steps upward, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar, based on the Ba'al Shem Tov, that one should pray for the Shechinah, which suffers in every Jewish pain. A parable about animals blaming a sheep shows how the world blames all Jews for one Jew's sin. He then explains 'sfas sheker' and 'lashon remiya', the holiness and power of the mouth, Meshech and Kedar, and the enemies who talk peace and mean war. On Tehillim 121 he teaches that help comes 'me'ayin', from above nature, when nothing else is left, illustrated by a story of the Ruzhiner, and closes with the Midrash on Yaakov Avinu robbed by Eliphaz.

en: The fifteen Shir Hamaalos are a sequence of ascent: the whole galus is a march up to Yerushalayim, and its troubles are steps toward the Beis HaMikdash.
Following the Bnei Yissaschar based on the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Rav teaches that in every pain of a Jew the Shechinah suffers with him, so one should pray for the Shechinah and then he too is helped.
'Sfas sheker' means even the edge of falsehood and 'lashon remiya' is deceit dressed up as kosher; the Rav says one must keep far even from the border of a lie.
Speech is what raises man above the animals; one who guards his mouth has great power in tefillah, while a mouth that is misused loses its power and makes a person worse than an animal.
The Rav reads 'me'ayin yavo ezri' as help that comes from 'nothing', from above nature: when a Jew sees there is no help left in this world, then Hashem's help comes.
The mountains to which one raises his eyes are the powers of this world, which cannot help; help is only from Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth, who is higher than them.

summary.en: After finishing Pesukei d'Zimra the Rav turns to the Shir Hamaalos, some of which are said on Shabbos. He brings the Gemara that David HaMelech said them when the waters rose from the foundations of the mizbe'ach, and that they correspond to the fifteen steps where the Levi'im sang, forming a sequence of ascent to the Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: Troubles of galus as steps upward

summary.en: On 'el Hashem batzarasa li karasi vaya'aneni' the Rav explains that galus is a march to Yerushalayim and its troubles are stepping stones. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar, based on the Ba'al Shem Tov, that the Shechinah shares every Jewish pain, so one should pray for the Shechinah, and notes how low the honor of Klal Yisrael has fallen today.

title.en: The parable of the sheep and the straw

summary.en: The Rav tells a humorous reading of the last passuk of Tehillim 119: in a plague among the animals the judges acquit the tiger and the wolf but convict the sheep that ate straw from a shoe. He applies it to the world, which excuses every sin of the nations but blames all Jews for the sin of one, and says the honor of Heaven has fallen very low.

title.en: Sfas sheker and lashon remiya

summary.en: The Rav says that a prayer for the Shechinah is answered only when it is sincere, and explains the next passuk: 'sfas sheker' is even the edge of a lie and 'lashon remiya' is deceit made to look kosher. He brings 'midvar sheker tirchak' and the Midrash that Hashem set guards on the mouth, and that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai wished man had two mouths.

title.en: The holiness and power of the mouth

summary.en: The Rav explains that one who guards his holy mouth has great power, so that his word is fulfilled and his tefillos answered, while a defiled mouth loses its power. Speech, the 'ruach memalela' given to Adam, is man's whole advantage over animals, so one who misuses it is worse than them.

title.en: Arrows of a warrior, and Meshech

summary.en: The Rav explains 'chitzei gibor shenunim im gachalei resamim': bad speech harms from far away like arrows, and lasts a long time like the coals of the broom tree. He then explains 'oya li ki garti meshech', identifying Meshech with the wild people of Russia.

title.en: Kedar and those who hate peace

summary.en: The Rav explains that Kedar are the Arabs, whom the Rambam calls the greatest liars, and that worse than dwelling with them is dwelling with a deceitful Jew. On 'ani shalom vechi adaber hemah lamilchamah' he describes leaders who speak peace to the Jews and war to their own people, and says David HaMelech is speaking of our times.

title.en: Shir lamaalos: help from 'ayin'

summary.en: The Rav notes that Tehillim 121 alone says 'shir lamaalos': it is a song to Hashem who goes with a Jew and lifts him up the steps. The mountains are the world's powers on which people rely, but help is only from Hashem; and through a Midrash on the word 'ayin' he explains that help comes from above nature when no other help remains.

title.en: The Ruzhiner and the turning wheel

summary.en: The Rav tells a story from the sefarim of Ruzhin: a chassid in deep trouble came weeping to the Ruzhiner, who told him of a merchant who wept when his lost money was found and danced when he had nothing left, because a wheel at the top must go down and at the bottom must rise. He ties it to 'me'ayin yavo ezri' and brings the Chesed L'Avraham that the geulah comes when Klal Yisrael can fall no lower.

title.en: The holy mountains and Yaakov's journey

summary.en: The Rav brings explanations that the mountains are the holy mountains of Yerushalayim, and that without Yerushalayim a Jew can still be helped by turning to the Maker of heaven and earth. He brings the Midrash that Yaakov Avinu said this Shir Hamaalos when Eliphaz took all his money, reading 'harim' as the Avos, and explains that the Avos' levels were taken from them so that they would hold on to Hashem from a low state and teach this to their children.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 121 and 122 as steps out of galus, the Rav teaches that Hashem, the Shomer Yisrael who never sleeps, watches every Jew with hashgacha pratis, and that hopes for the geulah held on to in the dark will one day be remembered with joy.

abstract.en: The Rav explains 'esa einai el heharim' as the cry of Jews who can no longer go up to the mountains of Zion: their help now comes directly from Hashem, Maker of 'heaven and earth', a name for the Beis Hamikdash, where the rules of number and nature did not apply. He brings the Midrash on Yaakov fleeing Esav with nothing, and reads 'He does not slumber' as Hashem staying awake through the sleep of galus. On 'Hashem is your shadow' he brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching of hashgacha pratis: Hashem acts toward a Jew as the Jew acts, and one who trusts this does not lose by davening and learning properly. He places these psalms at the darkest end of galus, likens it to Adar, and promises protection in success and light in darkness. On Tehillim 122 he brings Makkos 10a, a story from Yerushalayim about children who 'talked kugel', and the Midrash that the Jews in Egypt comforted themselves on Shabbos with the promise of redemption.

en: With the mountains of Zion destroyed, a Jew's help comes directly from Hashem, who made 'heaven and earth', the Beis Hamikdash that stood above the rules of number and nature.
Galus is like sleep, but the Shomer Yisrael never sleeps and guards the one sheep among seventy wolves.
'Hashem is your shadow': Hashem deals with a Jew the way the Jew conducts himself, so one who lives by hashgacha pratis is shown hashgacha pratis.
The Ba'al Shem Tov did not invent belief in hashgacha pratis but made it shine in his students' hearts, down to which way a falling straw points.
The end of galus is its darkest part, like the blackness before dawn and like Adar at the end of the year, yet it is just there that things turn over.
Whatever a Jew's circumstances, success or its opposite, Hashem arranges them for his good, and if he believes it is good Hashem will show him that it is.
The hopes Jews spoke of in the hard days of galus, on Shabbos in Egypt and in poverty in Yerushalayim, will be recalled with joy when they come true.

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash, often repeated by the Ba'al Shem Tov, that Hashem is a person's shadow and does what he does. A Jew who lives with hashgacha pratis does not cut short davening or learning for business, since he will not lose by serving Hashem, and he is shown hashgacha pratis openly.

title.en: Light that a teacher puts into a pasuk

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Ba'al haTanya brings a known Midrash in the Ba'al Shem Tov's name, and answers that he received its light from him. He illustrates with the Gemara's peddler and 'mi ha'ish hechafetz chaim', the sign of 'pakod pakadti', the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching on the falling straw, and a pasuk in Mishlei cited in a Tanna's name.

title.en: The darkest end of galus

summary.en: The Rav places the Shir Hamaalos at the end of galus, its darkest part, like the blackness before dawn and like Adar at the end of the year, when Hashem is hidden yet things turn over. He reads 'by day the sun will not strike you, nor the moon by night' for the nation through its bright and dark periods, and explains that every Jew can find himself in every pasuk of Tehillim.

title.en: Guarded in success and in darkness

summary.en: The Rav applies the end of the kapitel to the individual: one who fixes emunah in hashgacha pratis in himself is promised that his success will not harm him and that in his darkness Hashem will give him a moon. Hashem guards his going and coming forever, and arranges his circumstances for his good.

title.en: 'Samachti': remembering galus from the steps

summary.en: Starting Tehillim 122, the Rav brings the Gemara that people asked when David would die so the Beis Hamikdash could be built, and David rejoiced at it. He then reads the kapitel as the redeemed climbing the steps recalling how they comforted each other in galus, illustrated by a story he heard about poor children in Yerushalayim who asked their mother to 'talk kugel'.

title.en: Shabbos comfort in Egypt

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on 'v'al yishu b'divrei sheker': Moshe won the Jews a day of rest, and on Shabbos they gathered and comforted each other with scrolls of the promises of redemption, which Pharaoh called 'words of falsehood' when he demanded the same output without straw. He concludes that those hopes have come true and 'our feet are standing in your gates, Yerushalayim'.

catalogTitle: Miracles Enlighten the Darkness of עוה”ז

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that we live in a 'teivel', a world of confusion and hester panim, where Hashem's occasional revelations through tzaddikim are like lightning on a dark night, and our task is to believe even without seeing.

abstract.en: The Rav contrasts earlier generations, who saw open miracles from Yetzias Mitzrayim through the Beis HaMikdash, the Tannaim and later, with today's hester panim, which is our test of emunah. He brings the pasuk in Tehillim that Hashem's lightnings illuminated the 'teivel', and explains that teivel, one of the seven names of the earth, means confusion, as in the blemish 'tevallul' in Parshas Emor. Like a flash of lightning that shows a lost traveler the road on a dark, rainy night, Hashem sometimes lets tzaddikim reveal Him for a moment. He tells stories of tzaddikim who sensed what was hidden: the Slonimer Rebbe and the untoveled dishes, a gabbai and an untoveled knife, Rabbi Binyamin Diskin and a questionable chicken, and the Yeshuos Yaakov and a pancake made in a meat pan. He ends with the Kotzker Rebbe's answer to the Apta Rav, that believing is a higher level than seeing, and says our mission in this darkness is to believe.

en: Earlier generations saw open miracles, such as the ten miracles in the Beis HaMikdash, while today there is hester panim and our test is to have emunah without seeing.
The word 'teivel' in the pasuk of the lightnings means confusion, so the pasuk describes Hashem's lightning lighting up a world of confusion.
In today's hester panim tzaddikim are not given permission to show wonders as in earlier times, yet here and there a tzaddik does something that lights up the darkness for a moment.
Stories of tzaddikim who sensed untoveled vessels and forbidden food show that such people could see what is hidden.
Believing is a higher level than seeing, and the mission of our souls in this dark period is to believe in Hashem even though He disguises Himself.

summary.en: The Rav explains that teivel, one of the seven names of the earth, means confusion and mixture, as in the eye blemish 'tevallul' in Parshas Emor and the word used for forbidden unions. He gives the mashal of a traveler on a dark, rainy night whom a brief flash of lightning shows the road.

title.en: Glimpses through tzaddikim in a world of hiding

summary.en: The Rav applies the pasuk: we live in a teivel of hester panim where the wicked do as they please, and tzaddikim are not given permission to show wonders as before, yet occasionally a tzaddik's act lights up the dark for a moment. He mentions his own unexplainable experiences with tzaddikim, which he will not tell in public, and introduces the mussar chaburah in Williamsburg and the respected Yid who taught it.

title.en: The Slonimer Rebbe and the borrowed dishes

summary.en: The Rav retells a story witnessed by his mentor: when the Slonimer Rebbe visited Yerushalayim, he came to eat at the home of a poor, beardless chassid and would not eat, sensing that the dishes lent by a bearded neighbor had not been toveled. The Rebbe told the chassid that in Heaven they would ask him where his beard is, but of the neighbor they would ask where the Yid is.

title.en: The untoveled knife and the questionable chicken

summary.en: The Rav tells what Mr. Singer told him: a Rebbe's gabbai, a guest in his father's house, refused to cut the challah with a new knife that the boy had falsely claimed to have toveled. He then tells how the Rav of Brisk, given a chicken for the road by Rabbi Binyamin Diskin that turned out to be questionable, did not eat it.

title.en: The Yeshuos Yaakov's pancake; believing beyond seeing

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Yeshuos Yaakov avoided a butter pancake made in a meat pan, explaining it was no wonder but that the pancake had splashed him in the face. He concludes that such glimpses are rare lightning flashes in a deep hester panim, brings the machlokes of the Apta Rav and the Kotzker Rebbe over seeing or believing the ushpizin, and says our mission is to believe in Hashem despite His disguise.

oneLiner.en: Going through Tehillim 122, the Rav explains that Yerushalayim is built to match the Yerushalayim above, joins fear of Heaven with peace between people, stands above place, time and calculation, and is the name of every Jew, so a Jew must care about Jews everywhere.

abstract.en: The Rav reads Tehillim 122 verse by verse. 'Our feet stood in your gates' describes a person transfixed by the sight of the rebuilt city, and also the merit of those learning in Yerushalayim, which wins Israel's wars. 'Built like a city joined together' means Yerushalayim below is built to match Yerushalayim above, which is why, he says, the Old City's twisting streets were rebuilt exactly as before; nothing in holiness is random, just as Teveria's name and the shape of the human body each have a reason. The city's two names, from Shem and Avraham, join peace and fear of Heaven, matching the Chasam Sofer's point that Yerushalayim joins duties to Hashem and to people. The tribes rise there above their divisions to the level of Yaakov, and above place, time and calculation. The Davidic kings may sit in the Azarah because of their humility. Finally, 'ask for the peace of Yerushalayim' teaches that every Jew must care about Jews everywhere.

en: The Rav explains 'Yerushalayim habenuyah' to mean that Yerushalayim below is built exactly to match Yerushalayim and the Beis HaMikdash above.
He teaches that every matter of holiness is exactly as it is in Heaven and has a reason, from the streets of the Old City to the name Teveria and the structure of the human body.
Yerushalayim joins the two names Shem and Avraham gave it, peace and fear of Heaven, and so it joins duties between man and Hashem with duties between man and his fellow.
Yerushalayim was not divided among the tribes; it is the place of Yaakov, the trunk from which the tribes branch out, and in coming there the tribes were raised above their own level.
The Davidic kings could judge and sit in the Azarah because they were humble and nullified, so that they themselves are Yerushalayim.
Since all Jews are called Yerushalayim, 'ask for the peace of Yerushalayim' means a Jew must take interest in what happens to Jews everywhere.

summary.en: The Rav gives two readings of 'k'ir shechubrah lah yachdav': holiness breaks through its walls so that its surroundings join it, and Yerushalayim below is built to match Yerushalayim above, where Michael serves as kohen gadol. He connects this to the halachos of building the Mishkan and Mikdash and to the Rambam that all Yerushalayim has a din of Mikdash.

title.en: Why the Old City was rebuilt as it was

summary.en: The Rav describes the Old City after the Six-Day War, with its narrow twisting alleys, and how the man in charge of rebuilding it, a German Jew with a sense for history, rebuilt it street by street as before to preserve its antiquity. The Rav explains that Hashem put this idea into his head because Yerushalayim must match the Yerushalayim above, and everyone does Hashem's errand.

title.en: Nothing in holiness is by chance

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara's reason for the name Teveria, 'tovah re'iyasah', though Chazal knew the wicked Tiberius named it after himself, and the Rambam that the Sanhedrin will first return to Teveria. He then explains that the human body, the tzelem Elokim of 248 limbs, has a reason for every twist, as the face forms Hashem's Name, and so too the streets of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Fear of Heaven joined with peace

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yerushalayim joins the names given by two tzaddikim, Shalem by Shem and Yir'eh by Avraham. He brings the Chasam Sofer that some lands stress service of G-d and others only decency between people, while Yerushalayim holds both, as the next verses show: the tribes go up to thank Hashem, and the thrones of judgment are there.

title.en: The tribes rise to the place of Yaakov

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Yerushalayim was not divided among the tribes. Yaakov, linked with Shabbos, is the trunk and the tribes are the branches; Eretz Yisroel is the place of the tribes and Yerushalayim the place of Yaakov, so on the Yomim Tovim the tribes went up and were raised above the level of a tribe.

title.en: Above place, time and calculation

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yerushalayim is like an extension of Heaven, where the laws of mathematics do not apply: no one ever said the place was too crowded, those standing pressed together bowed with room to spare, and the Aron took up no space. The 'shivtei Kah' carry the Name Kah, which is above place, time and calculation.

title.en: The thrones of the House of David

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah that a king neither judges nor is judged, from the episode of Yannai and Shimon ben Shetach, while the Davidic kings could judge because they humbly stood to be judged; likewise only they may sit in the Azarah, because they are nullified to it. He explains bitul as a foundation of avodah, and resolves the Brisker Rav's question on the closing of the brachah for Yerushalayim: David is Yerushalayim.

title.en: Ask after the peace of every Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains 'sha'alu shalom Yerushalayim': the holiness of the Mikdash spreads over all Yerushalayim, and the Midrash calls all Jews Yerushalayim, so a Jew must take interest in Jews in Russia, Africa, Iraq and Teiman as one worries over a brother who stopped writing. He ends with 'for the sake of my brothers and friends' and 'for the sake of the House of Hashem', a prayer for both the place and the souls.

oneLiner.en: Going through Tehillim 123, 'Shir hamaalos elecha nasasi es einai', the Rav explains what it means that Hashem Himself is a Jew's mivtach, how a servant looks only to the hand that strikes him, and why Klal Yisrael cries out a double 'chaneinu' from the shame of galus.

abstract.en: The Rav reads 'elecha nasasi es einai hayoshvi bashamayim' as David HaMelech speaking for Klal Yisrael in galus. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov on 'vehayah Hashem mivtacho': a person must do his hishtadlus, but Hashem, not the business, must be the mivtach. Two stories illustrate it, the Ba'al Shem Tov knocking at a wealthy man's door and Reb Pinchas of Koretz throwing back a coin, and they explain Rashi on Yosef's two extra years in prison. 'Hayoshvi' means my own G-d in heaven, and bitachon must never stop. Like servants looking to their master's hand, a Jew who suffers turns to the One who sends the suffering. Through the hanging ayin of 'chazir miya'ar' he shows how galus can be turned around. The double 'chaneinu' is a reflexive cry, like 'maher maher' and Eliyahu's 'aneini aneini'. Finally, with Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch, he explains galus as a mission to the nations, borne with pride despite their scorn.

en: Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, a person must do hishtadlus, but Hashem Himself must be his mivtach, the one his hope rests on, not his business.
Yosef was kept two more years in prison for relying on the sar hamashkim because more is demanded of a tzaddik of his level.
'Hayoshvi bashamayim' expresses each Jew's personal G-d in heaven who watches over him with individual hashgachah, which gives him security.
Like a servant whose only hope is the master who strikes him, a Jew who suffers turns to Hashem who sends the suffering and asks Him for grace.
Repeated words in tefillah, 'maher maher' and the double 'chaneinu', are an inner cry, a reflex of a person who can no longer bear the pain, not an addition to the text.
Jews went into galus in the service of Hashem, to bring emunah and good middos to the nations, and they keep their pride and bitachon despite the nations' scorn.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov, Reb Pinchas of Koretz and Yosef

summary.en: The Rav tells how the young Ba'al Shem Tov knocked once at a wealthy man's door and left, having done his hishtadlus, and how Reb Pinchas of Koretz threw back a coin he found and then received it from a wealthy man. With the Biala Rebbe's comment and Rashi on Yosef's two extra years in prison, he explains that more is demanded of a tzaddik like Yosef.

title.en: My own G-d in heaven; bitachon without pause

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'hayoshvi' is not only ornament: Klal Yisrael says 'my One who sits in heaven', a personal G-d with individual hashgachah, and so feels secure. From the pause after 'einai' and the ta'amim he learns that a Jew's bitachon must continue without stop, even after he has done his part and even when by reason there is no hope.

title.en: Eyes of servants to the master's hand

summary.en: On 'hinei ke'einei avadim', the Rav explains that 'ad sheyechaneinu' asks for free grace, and brings the Radak: a servant struck by his master can hope only that the striking hand itself will stop and pardon him. So a Jew who suffers turns to Hashem who sends it; with 'im kevanim im ka'avadim' and the Kedushas Levi, Klal Yisrael asks to be treated again as children.

title.en: The hanging ayin of chazir miya'ar

summary.en: By way of drush the Rav brings 'yechar'semenah chazir miya'ar' with its raised ayin, and Rashi that the forest boar is Rome, which destroys when punishment is decreed on Israel. If Israel merits, the ayin becomes an aleph and the forest boar a helpless river creature; he connects this to the 'kosnos or' with an aleph in Rabbi Meir's Torah, and to the plea 'chaneinu Hashem chaneinu'.

title.en: The scorn of galus and the double 'maher'

summary.en: On 'ki rav savanu vuz' the Rav describes the nations' contempt, the doctrine that the Jews are cursed wanderers who will never have Yerushalayim, which he says is behind the uproar over Yerushalayim. He then asks how one may say 'maher maher' twice when the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, among them prophets, measured every word, and brings an example of an 'oy' cried out in the middle of davening.

title.en: A reflexive cry: 'quick, quick' and 'aneini aneini'

summary.en: The Rav gives a parable of a child outside who sees a tiger and cries 'Father, quick!' and then 'quick!' again: the second cry adds nothing, it is a reflex like 'ouch'. So the second 'maher' and the second 'chaneinu' are an inner cry, and he shows the same from the Gemara in Taanis on Eliyahu's 'aneini aneini', where the second word is the cry.

title.en: Turning the cheek; sated with scorn

summary.en: The Rav brings a later author on 'yiten lemakeihu lechi yisba becherpah': when the one struck offers his cheek, the striker is satisfied with the disgrace and stops striking. So Klal Yisrael says it is already sated with the shame of galus, 'rabbas sav'ah lah nafsheinu', the mockery of the complacent nations and the scorn toward the defenseless dove.

title.en: Galus as a mission; proud beggars

summary.en: Following Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch, the Rav explains that Jews are in galus in Hashem's service, to be a light to the nations; in Shlomo's time the nations came to them, and now, not having merited, Jews must go to the nations, as he brings from the Chasam Sofer and the Gemara. In that service they bear scorn but keep their pride and bitachon, mocked as 'proud beggars', until Hashem brings them back to Tziyon.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות ... לולי ה' שהיה לנו

oneLiner.en: Through Tehillim 124 and 125, the Rav explains that the Jewish people survive their exile because they recognize Hashem's hand in everything and trust in Him, and that their holiness, like Yerushalayim's, comes from the Shechinah and can never be taken away.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a remez on why the first blessing of Shemoneh Esrei says 'Elokei Yaakov' and not Yisrael, then reads Tehillim 124. Only a Jew who sees Hashem's providence in everything can say 'Had Hashem not been with us'. He brings the Gemara that 'a man rose against us' means Haman, a man with free choice rather than a king, and explains the floods, Rashi on the splitting of all waters at the Yam Suf, and the trap that broke. The nations that fought the Jews were broken, while the Jews revived again and again; he describes the sinking of pre-war American Jewry like Pisom and Raamses, tells of a Jew who would not work on Shabbos, and the rebirth of Torah after the war. 'Our help is in Hashem's Name' means recognizing that He constantly renews creation. In Tehillim 125 he explains Har Tziyon and, with the Rambam, that Yerushalayim's and Klal Yisrael's holiness comes from the Shechinah and is never annulled.

en: Only a Jew for whom Hashem's Name is constantly on his lips, who sees Hashem's providence in everything, can say 'Had Hashem not been with us', unlike the nations who credit luck.
The Gemara reads 'a man rose against us' as Haman: a man has free choice and is harder to be saved from than a king, whose heart is in Hashem's hand.
The nations that attacked the Jews were all broken in the end, while the Jewish people survived and revived after every trouble, including after the Nazis.
Jews survive in exile through recognizing that Hashem is with them and runs the world; the more they know it, the more help they have.
Those who trust in Hashem are like Har Tziyon, which never moves; even in exile they are protected as the mountains surround Yerushalayim.

According to the Rambam, Yerushalayim's holiness comes from the Shechinah and was never annulled; Klal Yisrael's holiness likewise comes from the Shechinah dwelling among them and no conquest or sin can take it away.

title.en: Who can say 'Had Hashem not been with us'

summary.en: The Rav opens with a remez from sefarim on why Shemoneh Esrei says 'Elokei Yaakov' rather than Yisrael, then reads the start of Tehillim 124. He asks who it is that says 'Had Hashem not been with us' and answers: a Jew who sees Hashem's providence in everything, unlike the nations who speak of luck.

title.en: Haman, the floods and the broken trap

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that 'a man rose against us' is Haman and explains why a man with free choice is more dangerous than a king. He explains the floods as forces of judgment that split before the Jews by the eternal power of the Yam Suf, and the bird escaping the broken trap, which the meforshim apply to the Beis HaMikdash; the nations that fought the Jews were all broken.

title.en: Pre-war America like Pisom and Raamses

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the unrecognized wonder of Torah's growth after the Nazi destruction, and contrasts pre-war America, which he likens to Pisom and Raamses built on sinking ground. He tells that of about forty boys in his yeshiva class only four remained Shabbos-observant, and describes the immigrants who had to work on Shabbos to keep a job.

title.en: Holding on to Shabbos in America

summary.en: The Rav tells of a Williamsburg Jew who would not work on Shabbos, and of an old Jew who, ready to give in for his family's sake, saw bread in a garbage can and resolved not to work on Shabbos as long as there was bread there; in the end Hashem helped him. He adds that those who could got a pushcart license, while millions sank and their children did not stay Jewish.

title.en: The rebirth after the war

summary.en: The Rav describes how the youth of his own shul sank, and how after the war refugees and great leaders like the Satmar Rav, the Klausenburger Rav, Rabbi Yonasan Steif and the Vizhnitzer Rebbe rebuilt Yiddishkeit here and in Eretz Yisrael. He calls it a techiyas hameisim of a people that is taken for granted, and explains that the trap broke and the Jews came out whole, not like a bird that escapes with a broken wing.

title.en: What sustains the Jews in exile

summary.en: The Rav asks what keeps the Jews alive in exile and answers from the opening and close of the kapitel: recognizing that Hashem is with us and runs the world, 'our help is in the Name of Hashem, Maker of heaven and earth'. 'Maker' in the present means He constantly renews creation, so that, as the talmidei haBa'al Shem Tov say, a decree can be absent from the new heavens. He then begins Tehillim 125: those who trust in Hashem are like Har Tziyon, built on rock, which never moves.

title.en: Tziyon as a mark of G-dliness

summary.en: The Rav explains that the mountains around Yerushalayim are a natural protection, and so Hashem surrounds His people. He brings Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch that Tziyon means a marker: from there the knowledge of one G-d went out into the world, and those who trust in Hashem take over that role in exile, firm and unmoving.

title.en: Holiness that comes from the Shechinah

summary.en: The Rav explains the Rambam's view that the holiness of Eretz Yisrael that came from Yehoshua's conquest was annulled when Nevuchadnetzar conquered it, but Yerushalayim's holiness comes from the Shechinah and remains. So too Klal Yisrael is holy because the Shechinah dwells among them, and no conquest by the nations can remove it. A Jew who knows this, that he is a part of G-d above, will not sin and drag the Shechinah into exile.

catalogTitle: The Multitudes at הר סיני - An Iron Proof of the Truth of the תורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the emunah of Klal Yisrael rests not on the word of one man but on what millions of people saw together at Har Sinai and in the Midbar, a testimony that could never have been fabricated.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with emunas tzaddikim, belief in tzaddikim alongside belief in Hashem, and says tzaddikim know everything because everything is in the Torah. He illustrates this with the story of the Ramban and his student Avner, who found his name hinted in a passuk of Haazinu, and with the Chazon Ish, who guided surgeons from his knowledge of Hilchos Treifos. The Torah is the blueprint of the world, and it also foretells the future: the division of Eretz Yisrael, the promise that nobody will covet a man's land when he goes up to Yerushalayim, galus, and the survival of the Jewish people and of the Torah while the empires that oppressed them vanished. After a question on Rashi's first comment, he turns to the catalog's theme. Christianity and Islam each began with one man whom people believed. Jewish emunah rests on millions who stood at Har Sinai and lived through forty years of open miracles, recorded in a Torah that every Jew received and that was copied identically across the world.

en: Emunah includes emunas tzaddikim: believing in Moshe Rabbeinu and the tzaddikim, not only in Hashem.
Everything in the world is in the Torah, because Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world; this is how tzaddikim know everything.
The Torah foretells the future, from the division of Eretz Yisrael to galus and the eternal survival of the Jewish people and the Torah.
An event witnessed by a multitude, such as the existence of a president or of Alexander the Great, cannot be fabricated or denied.
Christianity and Islam rest on the word of one person; Jewish emunah rests on the experience of millions at Har Sinai.
The Torah, written at the end of forty years in the Midbar, recorded what the whole people had experienced and was copied letter for letter by every Jew down the generations.
