title.en: Emunas tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav opens with emunas tzaddikim: at Kriyas Yam Suf the Jews believed in Hashem and in Moshe His servant. He says he has himself seen the ruach hakodesh of tzaddikim, and that tzaddikim know everything because everything is in the Torah.

title.en: The Ramban and Avner in Haazinu

summary.en: The Rav tells the story of the Ramban's student Avner, who went off the derech, challenged the Ramban's teaching that Haazinu contains every Jew's history, and was shown his name in the third letters of a passuk. Shaken, Avner did teshuvah and set off in a boat without oars.

title.en: Everything is in the Torah

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Chazon Ish showed surgeons how to perform brain surgery, saying he knew it from Hilchos Treifos. He brings the Ramban that Shlomo HaMelech knew everything from the Torah, explains that the Torah is the blueprint of creation, and notes that the Zohar says the world is round. He adds that, unlike other religions' books, the Torah foretells the future, and it was given identically to all of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: The Torah's promises come true

summary.en: The Rav shows the Torah foretelling the future: the nachalos of the shevatim and Yehoshua's conquest; the promise that nobody will covet a man's land when he goes up to Yerushalayim three times a year; galus and the survival of the Jews while Bavel, Paras, Yavan and Rome disappeared; and that the Torah will not be forgotten, as seen in the growth of Torah learning after the war.

title.en: A question on the first Rashi

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's first comment on Bereishis, that the Torah should have begun with the mitzvah of Rosh Chodesh, the first mitzvah given to Yisrael, and asks how it can be called the first when milah, and according to one opinion gid hanasheh, were commanded earlier.

title.en: What a multitude witnessed cannot be denied

summary.en: The Rav sets out why we believe: of the three main religions, Christianity and Islam accept the Torah but claim Hashem changed His mind. He then builds the principle that an event witnessed by hundreds of thousands cannot be fabricated, using President Ford, George Washington, Julius Caesar and Alexander the Great, whom the Gemara mentions meeting Shimon HaTzaddik.

title.en: Religions built on one man

summary.en: The Rav describes how Christianity began with one charismatic man whose teaching, built on Judaism, people believed, and how Islam began with Mohammed, whom the Rambam calls a madman, whose book contradicts recorded history. In both cases people believed one person.

title.en: Millions at Har Sinai

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Jews do not believe because Moshe said so, but because a few million people stood at Har Sinai and heard Hashem. The Torah, written at the end of forty years, recorded the miracles they all lived through, every Jew was commanded to have a Sefer Torah, and the Torah was copied letter for letter so that Jews cut off from each other for centuries hold the identical text.

oneLiner.en: Through the last verses of Shir HaMa'alos HaBotchim and the opening of Shir HaMa'alos B'shuv, the Rav explains why tzaddikim accept Heaven's decrees, why each soul is held to the Torah at its own level, and why the redemption will be 'like a dream'.

abstract.en: The Rav explains 'the rod of the wicked will not rest on the lot of the tzaddikim': the rule of the wicked is only temporary, so tzaddikim do not raise their hands against it. He shows this in the tzaddikim of the Spanish expulsion, the Ten Martyrs, the tzaddikim of the war years and a story of the Ruzhiner. On 'do good to the good and the upright in heart' he contrasts true good people with hypocrites, and tells how the Kotzker eased a scoffer out of Rebbe Reb Bunim's chevra. From the washing of hands in the morning he develops that souls and Torah have levels: the Shulchan Aruch is the minimum, and for a higher person lifnim mishuras hadin becomes the law, as in the story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah. Therefore one should not mock the chumros of greater Jews. Finally he gives several explanations of 'we were like dreamers'.

en: The rule of the wicked over the tzaddikim is only temporary, so tzaddikim do not stretch out their hands to fight it but accept the decree and rely on Hashem.
Great tzaddikim who had the power to overturn kingdoms asked in Heaven, were told it was a decree, and accepted it.
David HaMelech asks Hashem to do good to those who are upright through and through, and to lead the crooked hypocrites away so they do not mix with honest Jews.
Souls and the Torah both have levels; the Shulchan Aruch is the minimum, and each person must keep the Torah according to his level.
What is lifnim mishuras hadin (beyond the letter of the law) for an ordinary person is the law itself for a person of a higher level.
One should not mock or criticize chumros of greater Jews or of a Rebbe's followers, since they stem from a higher level or from bond to the Rebbe.
'We were like dreamers' means that the redemption will surpass every dream, and that its joy will make the whole galus seem like a dream.

title.en: The rod of the wicked is only temporary

summary.en: The Rav explains that the rule of the wicked over the tzaddikim is temporary, so tzaddikim do not raise their hands against it but rely on Hashem. He brings the tzaddikim of the Spanish expulsion, who could have overturned Spain but were told in Heaven it was a decree and accepted it.

title.en: The Ten Martyrs, the war years and the Ruzhiner

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Ten Martyrs, who could have destroyed Rome, let themselves be killed, and answers that Heaven told them it was the decree. He adds the tzaddikim of the war who accepted the decree, and tells how the Ruzhiner, fleeing the Czar, did not use his power against Russia because Russia had once taken in fleeing Jews.

title.en: The truly good and the hypocrites

summary.en: On 'do good, Hashem, to the good and to the upright in their hearts' the Rav explains that the good are those who are good through and through, unlike hypocrites who only put on a fine face. David HaMelech asks that the crooked be led away from the honest, and the Rav begins the account of Rebbe Reb Bunim's chevra of great minds.

title.en: The Kotzker and the scoffer

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Kotzker saw that a brilliant newcomer lacked emunas tzaddikim and mocked the Ba'er Heitev's words on walking without washing the hands, and gently persuaded him to leave the chevra. He returns to the verse, 'lead them away... peace upon Israel', and to the care Chassidim take with washing the hands at the bed.

title.en: Levels of souls and levels of Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that pshat, remez, drush and sod correspond to nefesh, ruach, neshamah and chayah, so both a stringent sefer and a lenient posek are right, each for its level. The Shulchan Aruch is the minimum; Yerushalayim, being higher, was destroyed for keeping only the letter of the law. A stain that does not matter on a potato sack ruins silk, and a Gemara that seems exaggerated speaks of a higher person.

title.en: For a higher person, beyond the law is the law

summary.en: From the steps to the mizbe'ach counted as uncovering nakedness, the Rav shows that for an oved Hashem pride is like giluy arayos. He tells the Gemara's story of Rabbah bar bar Chanah and the porters, where Rav told him that for him lifnim mishuras hadin is the law, and reads 'v'eileh hamishpatim asher tasim lifneihem' the same way. He applies it to waiting between meat and milk.

title.en: The Belzer Rav's grapes; do not mock chumros

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Belzer Rav, who would not eat grapes a host in Boro Park had obtained for him in winter, because the plate had not been toiveled. He concludes that one must not mock or criticize the chumros of greater Jews, and brings the Gemara in Sukkah that Rav Kahana's students followed even his leniency on hadassim as a bond to their Rebbe.

title.en: 'We were like dreamers'

summary.en: The Rav opens Shir HaMa'alos B'shuv and gives several explanations of 'we were like dreamers': the redemption will exceed all we imagined, as real food exceeds a prisoner's dream; it will be like the impossible sights of a dream; its joy will make galus seem a dream; and, in a pshat he attributes to Rav Shimshon Raphael Hirsch, we will then discover the tikunim Jews achieved for the world in galus.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות בשוב ה' את שיבת ציון

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Shir HaMa'alos, 'B'shuv Hashem es shivas Tziyon', as the joy of a geulah that will make the long galus seem like a dream and reveal that the Jews' greatness, influence and tears in exile were all planting for the redemption, and then turns to 'Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo' and why the Beis HaMikdash built by man had to be destroyed.

abstract.en: The Rav reads 'B'shuv Hashem es shivas Tziyon hayinu k'cholmim': the geulah will exceed all dreams, and the bitter galus will pass like a dream one wakes from. In galus Jews feel mocked and powerless, yet their influence, which he explains through Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky's reading of the word hashpa'ah, flows down on the nations and on less observant Jews, as the Rambam shows; this is the 'light to the nations'. Citing Rebbe Nachman, he says the greatness is with the Jews even now, and when Moshiach comes the Jews will laugh at the nations' limited understanding. He describes the longing in 'Shuvah Hashem es shevisenu', the Ba'al HaTanya's teaching that thirst in galus exceeds that of Temple times, and the tears that are seeds of the geulah, with Rebbe Zusha's vort on sowing in tears or in joy. He then turns to 'Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo': the Beis HaMikdash built by human hands had to fall, all within Hashem's plan, so that the Kosel Maaravi and its kedushah would remain.

en: The geulah will surpass every dream, and the long galus will then seem like a passing dream.
Even when Jews feel powerless and mocked in galus, their influence flows down on the nations and on less observant Jews, and this is why Hashem sent them into galus, to be a light to the nations.
The true greatness is with the Jews even in galus; when Moshiach comes this will be revealed, and the nations' limited grasp of it will be cause for laughter.
The longing of Jews in galus is greater than in Temple times, and that longing, with their Torah, tefillos and tears, is itself the seed that brings the geulah.
The Beis HaMikdash built by human hands could not last; its destruction was part of Hashem's plan, and the true Beis HaMikdash Hashem Himself will build.

According to the Yismach Moshe, the Beis HaMikdash was built so that, after its destruction, the Kosel Maaravi would remain, where the Shechinah stays and on which the Jews' existence in galus depends.

title.en: The geulah will be like a dream

summary.en: After a false start, the Rav begins 'B'shuv Hashem es shivas Tziyon hayinu k'cholmim' and explains that the geulah will exceed all dreams, while the bitter galus will pass like a dream one wakes from. The great prophecies of the nevi'im, he says, are nothing compared to what will actually be.

title.en: The hidden influence of Jews in galus

summary.en: The Rav describes how in galus Jews feel they accomplish nothing, surrounded by enemies and scoffers who mock even ehrliche Yidden. He explains, through Rav Yaakov Kamenetsky's reading of the word hashpa'ah, that their influence flows down on the nations and on less observant Jews, and that this is the purpose of galus, to be a light to the nations, as seen in the Rambam.

title.en: Then our mouths will fill with laughter

summary.en: On 'Az yimalei s'chok pinu' the Rav says the Jews will laugh last, and their speech will turn to song. Bringing Rebbe Nachman of Breslov and a mashal of a prince disciplined by servants, he explains that the greatness is with the Jews even in galus, and that when Moshiach comes the nations will grasp it only in a limited way, which is why the Jews will laugh at them.

title.en: Longing for the geulah like streams in the Negev

summary.en: The Rav explains 'Shuvah Hashem es shevisenu' as a tefilah said with thirst and longing for the days of Moshiach, a longing he says has weakened even among bnei Torah, and brings the Midrash that the Jews in Mitzrayim spoke on Shabbos of the coming redemption. He explains 'ka'afikim banegev' and brings the Ba'al HaTanya that the thirst of Jews in galus for Hashem is greater than in the time of the Beis HaMikdash, like a person in a desert compared with one who knows water is at hand.

title.en: Sowing in tears, reaping in joy

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah, avodah, tefillos, longing and tears of Jews in galus are seeds of the geulah, and that even in galus Jews rejoiced, like a sheep among seventy wolves. He brings Rebbe Zusha's vort on serving Hashem with tears or with joy, and the Midrash that Israel in galus is called Yizre'el, planting belief in Hashem among the nations, for which they will be rewarded when galus ends.

title.en: Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo and the first Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Rav turns to 'Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo', which Dovid HaMelech composed about the Beis HaMikdash his son would build and which would not last, and retells from Chazal how Shlomo's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter delayed the morning tamid and how Gavriel planted the reed from which Rome grew. He insists Shlomo is not understood and acted l'shem shamayim, and explains 'Im Hashem lo yivneh bayis': only what Hashem builds endures.

title.en: A Mikdash built by man had to fall

summary.en: Bringing Rashi on 'Mikdash Hashem konenu yadecha' and something he heard from a tzaddik, the Rav explains that the Beis HaMikdash was destroyed because a human hand built it; Shlomo only appears to be the cause. Like the sale of Yosef, the sin of the Eitz HaDa'as and the meraglim, it was all in Hashem's plan, which will be understood when Moshiach comes. He adds Rashi's explanation that the third Beis HaMikdash will come down from heaven.

title.en: Built to leave the Kosel Maaravi

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yismach Moshe that the Beis HaMikdash was built to be destroyed so that the Kosel Maaravi would remain, where the Shechinah never departs, and the Arvei Nachal that all the kedushah of the Mikdash lies hidden under the Kosel. He closes with the Rambam that the kedushah of Yerushalayim and the Mikdash is never nullified, since it comes from the Shechinah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Shir HaMa'alos l'Shlomo and the next chapter, Ashrei kol yerei Hashem: everything depends on Hashem's help, children are a blessing and a source of parnassah, and the happiness of a Jew lies in a home run by the Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the psalm David HaMelech composed for Shlomo about the Beis HaMikdash: because Shlomo slept late on the night before its inauguration, the churban was already set in motion, and 'if Hashem does not build the house' speaks of that destruction. A house, a city and a livelihood all need siyata dishmaya. He applies 'it is vain for you who rise early' to people who give all their strength to business and leave no time for davening and learning, bringing the Midrash about the mann. He then explains that some events are part of Hashem's plan from before creation, so Shlomo is not to be blamed, and David calls him a gift from Hashem. In a second reading the chapter is about bitachon: children bring parnassah, youth is precious like arrows in a warrior's hand, and even the mud children bring in is a blessing. Finally, he explains chapter 128: the happiness of an honest, content Jewish home, a modest wife and children around the table.

en: The Rav explains that 'if Hashem does not build the house' speaks of the destruction of the Beis HaMikdash, which began with Shlomo sleeping late on the night before its inauguration.
A person, a household, a city and a business all need siyata dishmaya; without it effort is in vain.
Those who rise early and stay up late for business, leaving no time for proper davening and learning, labor in vain, because what is decreed for a person he will receive.
Some events, like the churban, Moshe not entering Eretz Yisrael and the sale of Yosef, were set in Hashem's plan before creation, so they are not a punishment and Shlomo is not to be blamed.
For a G-d-fearing Jew children are a blessing: each child brings a new channel of parnassah.
The years of youth are precious, like arrows in a warrior's hand: once they have passed they cannot be recaptured.
Chapter 128 shows the happiness of a Jew who lives by the Torah: honest earnings, a modest wife, children around the table, and contentment in this world and the next.

title.en: A psalm for Shlomo about the Beis HaMikdash

summary.en: The Rav explains that David composed this psalm for Shlomo about the Beis HaMikdash, which was destroyed because it began badly: Shlomo slept late on the night before its inauguration. 'If Hashem does not build the house' speaks of the churban, and he concludes that a person, a home and a city all need siyata dishmaya.

title.en: Rising early for business in vain

summary.en: The Rav applies 'it is vain for you who rise early' to people who pour all their strength into business and leave no time for davening, learning and their children's chinuch. He brings the Midrash about the mann and a tzaddik's question to a man running to his livelihood, and says business needs no hiddurim; a Jew with bitachon lives an orderly life and eats his bread with simcha.

title.en: Hashem's plan, and Shlomo is not to blame

summary.en: The Rav asks how David could speak this way about his son Shlomo, and answers that some things are part of Hashem's plan from before creation and are not a punishment, citing the Ohr HaChaim and the Midrash Tanchuma: Moshe and the rock, Adam and the Eitz HaDa'as, the sale of Yosef and the two churbanos. Only by the greatest tzaddikim does this happen, and so David continues 'behold, children are the heritage of Hashem', proud of his son Shlomo.

title.en: Bitachon: children bring parnassah

summary.en: In a second reading the Rav explains the chapter as speaking of bitachon. People who calculate their budget see children as a burden, and secular Israelis mock large families, but for a G-d-fearing Jew each child is a blessing that opens a new channel of parnassah; he tells how this was so in his own home. Children are 'like arrows in a warrior's hand', helping their parents.

title.en: The precious years of youth

summary.en: The Rav brings the words of the Kotzker and a letter of the Chiddushei HaRim to his grandson: one year of youth is worth many later years. A young person can still bend his middos like a young tree and retains what he learns; once youth passes, like an arrow shot from the bow, it cannot be recaptured.

title.en: A quiver full of children, and the muddy floor

summary.en: The Rav explains 'fortunate is the man who fills his quiver' as a home full of children who will be arrows in avodas Hashem, and adds a light pshat that even the mud children bring into the house is a great blessing. He tells of a tzaddik in self-imposed galus whose muddy shoes upset a rebbetzin, and his reply that she had mercy on the floor instead of on people, and concludes that one needs priorities.

title.en: Ashrei kol yerei Hashem: the honest Jewish home

summary.en: Turning to chapter 128, the Rav brings the Radak that 'kol' includes the woman, and Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch's reading that David takes a stranger into a Jewish home and town to show its warmth and contentment. He explains 'the toil of your hands' as honestly earned bread, and with the Gemara reads 'fortunate' as this world and 'good for you' as the World to Come.

title.en: The fruitful vine and the olive saplings

summary.en: The Rav explains the modest wife who is content within the home and on whom the whole house stands, and the children like evergreen olive saplings around the table, with a family that eats together and needs no outside sensations. He concludes that only for a yerei Hashem is all this a blessing; to others it means nothing.

catalogTitle: “משה אב לנביאים” - the Root of the Yiddishe Mesorah

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, from the Rambam, that our emunah in the Torah rests not on Moshe Rabbeinu's miracles but on the whole nation hearing Hashem appoint him at Har Sinai, so that every mitzvah and every other navi is believed only through Moshe Rabbeinu.

abstract.en: Continuing from last week, the Rav reads the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter 8: Klal Yisroel did not believe in Moshe Rabbeinu because of his signs, since a sign can always leave a doubt that it was a trick; the signs in the midbar were done because they were needed. They believed because at Har Sinai every Jew was a navi and heard Hashem speak to Moshe and appoint him. Therefore a navi who performs wonders to contradict Moshe is not heard, like witnesses who claim it is night when the beis din sees it is day. Listening to any other navi is a mitzvah, like listening to two witnesses, and not proof. The Rav reads a letter in the Igros Moshe on why a tradition seen by a multitude cannot be false. He closes by answering Rashi's question on the first mitzvah, and explains the Ani Maamin that Moshe is the father of all the nevi'im.

en: According to the Rambam, Klal Yisroel's belief in Moshe Rabbeinu was not based on his signs, because a sign always leaves a small doubt that it was a trick.
At Har Sinai every Jew was a navi and heard Hashem speak to Moshe and appoint him to give the rest of the Torah; this is the basis of believing in him.
A navi who shows wonders in order to contradict Moshe Rabbeinu's nevuah is not listened to, just as two witnesses who say it is night are not believed when the beis din sees it is day.
Listening to any other navi is a mitzvah under the Torah's conditions, like listening to witnesses, not a certainty; only Moshe Rabbeinu's nevuah is beyond doubt.
A tradition that a multitude saw with their own eyes cannot be false, since a lie about something that hundreds of thousands witnessed would be exposed at once.
Every mitzvah, even milah, and every navi before or after Moshe is accepted only because Moshe Rabbeinu transmitted it, which is why he is called the father of all the nevi'im.

title.en: Not belief through signs

summary.en: The Rav recalls that our emunah rests on a mesorah the whole nation saw, and reads the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter 8 that Klal Yisroel did not believe in Moshe Rabbeinu because of his signs. He compares a sign to a magician's trick that still leaves a doubt, and explains that the signs in the midbar were done because they were needed.

title.en: All Yidden were nevi'im at Sinai

summary.en: The Rav explains that at Matan Torah every Jew was a navi and heard Hashem speak to Moshe and appoint him, as the pesukim in Shemos promise. Therefore a navi who performs wonders to refute Moshe Rabbeinu is not heard, like witnesses who say it is night while the beis din sees it is day.

title.en: Listening to a navi is like listening to witnesses

summary.en: The Rav explains that a navi may command a temporary deviation, as Eliyahu offered korbanos on Har Hakarmel, but never avodah zarah. Listening to such a navi is a mitzvah like accepting two witnesses, which is not foolproof, as the case of Navos shows; only Moshe Rabbeinu's nevuah, which the whole nation saw and heard, is certain.

title.en: A letter on proving the Torah true

summary.en: The Rav sums up the Rambam and reads a letter from the Igros Moshe to someone troubled by doubts about the truth of the Torah. The answer is not philosophy but the mesorah of a multitude: a father cannot tell his son he saw something together with 600,000 people if nobody else saw it, and even the nations accept the miracles of Mitzrayim and the midbar.

title.en: The first mitzvah and Moshe av lanevi'im

summary.en: The Rav returns to Rashi's question why the Torah did not begin with HaChodesh hazeh lachem, the first mitzvah, though milah and gid hanasheh came earlier. He answers that those mitzvos are known only because Moshe told us about them, so HaChodesh hazeh is the first mitzvah heard from Moshe, and explains the Ani Maamin that Moshe is the father of all nevi'im before and after him.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות אשרי כל ירא ה'

oneLiner.en: Learning Tehillim 128 and 129, the Rav explains that one who fears Hashem sanctifies even his physical life and his home, which draws its blessing from the beis medrash and Tziyon, while the nations' hatred of Tziyon comes from envy and leaves them without roots or blessing.

abstract.en: The Rav opens Tehillim 128 with 'haholech bidrachav': the covenant with Noach was a heavenly sign, while the covenant of milah lets a Jew serve Hashem with his very body. Walking in Hashem's ways, even while still on the way, makes the body a sanctuary. He reads the blessings of the Jewish home: the wife as a vine that cannot be grafted, the children rooted at home who bear fruit outside, and the content man who is never bored. With Rav Hirsch he adds that the home's root is the beis knesses, 'Hashem will bless you from Tziyon', and stresses seeing the good of Yerushalayim, with stories of the Chasam Sofer and Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld and a warning about false zealotry. Turning to Tehillim 129, he describes Jewish suffering since its youth, the empires that vanished, and the nations' envy, the true reason for their hatred. Their end is grass on the roofs, without roots and without blessing, which Rav Shmelke of Nikolsburg applies to those who hate talmidei chachamim, illustrated by a story from Belz.

en: The covenant with Noach was a sign in the heavens, while the covenant of milah lets a Jew serve Hashem with his physical body, which the bnei Noach cannot do.
'Haholech bidrachav' means that one who fears Hashem is praiseworthy even while still on the way, and by walking in Hashem's ways his body becomes a sanctuary for Him.
The man who fears Hashem is content in his home and never bored, unlike those who chase sensations outside.
The beis knesses and beis medrash are the main part of a Jew's home, and from there the private home draws its blessing, 'Hashem will bless you from Tziyon'.
One must see the good of Yerushalayim; criticism must be constructive, and zealotry is only for one who has checked himself that he means only Heaven's sake.
The nations' hatred of the Jews has no reason in Jewish deeds; it comes from envy, a sense that the Jews are better and have a future.
The haters of Tziyon are like grass on the roofs, without roots or a future, and no one passing gives them a blessing.

title.en: The covenant of Noach and the covenant of milah

summary.en: The Rav opens Tehillim 128 with 'haholech bidrachav' and contrasts the covenant with Noach, a rainbow in the sky, with Avraham's covenant of milah. The mitzvos of the bnei Noach are spiritual only, while milah is a covenant in the flesh, letting a Jew serve Hashem with his physical functions.

title.en: Walking in His ways makes the body a sanctuary

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on 'Uri tzafon uvo'i seiman' about korbanos and the eating of shelamim, physical acts that serve Hashem. He explains that one is a 'holech' even before reaching the goal, as a hava amina in Gemara is also Torah, and that walking in Hashem's ways, being compassionate and gracious as He is, makes the body a sanctuary.

title.en: The vine, the olive saplings and the content man

summary.en: The Rav explains 'eshtecha kegefen poriyah': a vine cannot be grafted, which is the purity of the Jewish home, and with the Radak, a vine planted inside the house sends its fruit outside, as children rooted in the home sanctify Hashem's name outside. The man who fears Hashem is blessed and content with his family, never bored, unlike those who chase sensations.

title.en: The private home and the collective home

summary.en: Following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, the Rav says the psalm brings the reader into the Jewish home, where the Shechinah rests. He then explains 'yevarechecha Hashem miTziyon': the beis knesses and beis medrash are the collective home and the main source of blessing, and their spirit, like that of Yerushalayim, is brought into the private home.

title.en: Seeing the good of Yerushalayim

summary.en: On 'ur'eh betuv Yerushalayim' the Rav brings Rav Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld's call to see the good of Yerushalayim, the sin of the meraglim, and a story of the Chasam Sofer. He tells of two brothers to show that zealotry must be purely for Heaven's sake, and closes the psalm: a home rooted in the beis knesses continues Yiddishkeit for generations, 'shalom al Yisrael'.

title.en: 'Rabbas tzeraruni': oppressed since youth

summary.en: Turning to Tehillim 129, the Rav describes Jewish history as full of decrees and persecution, and asks why great empires bother with a tiny nation. The empires that oppressed the Jews have long vanished, and he explains 'al gabi charshu chorshim' with the image of an ox plowing long furrows without rest.

title.en: Hashem cuts the ropes; hatred born of envy

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem, being a tzaddik, cut the ropes with which the nations harnessed the Jews to their plow, and the haters of Tziyon will retreat in shame, as Charvona turned around when Haman fell. Going back to the beginning of Jewish history shows no reason for the hatred; citing a commentary on 'vayekan'u vo echav', he says the nations hate the Jews out of envy.

title.en: Grass on the roofs, without a blessing

summary.en: The Rav explains 'yihyu kachatzir gagos': growth on a roof has no soil, dries out before it is pulled, and does not fill the reaper's hand, like the nations who have no roots, no true way of life and no future. Passersby give no blessing to such a crop, as one should bless a Jew at his work.

title.en: Rav Shmelke on gilgulim and the Belzer kugel

summary.en: The Rav brings Rav Shmelke of Nikolsburg: the 'haters of Tziyon' are those who hate the talmid chacham, and a soul reincarnated in food finds its tikkun when a Jew makes a brachah over it, which the hater will not merit. He illustrates this with Rav Sholom of Belz, who had a fallen piece of Shabbos kugel picked up and eaten, and ends that one who loves talmidei chachamim is guided by Hashem to a Jewish table.

oneLiner.en: Returning to Tehillim 128, the Rav explains that through the Shabbos and Chanukah lights every Jewish home becomes a Beis HaMikdash that Yerushalayim comes to visit, and that Chanukah is a time of growth in Torah and of thanking Hashem.

abstract.en: The Rav announces Tehillim 129 but returns to 128, which, following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, shows the warmth and contentment of the Jewish home, and reads 'Hashem will bless you from Zion' as the shul, the communal home. Since it is Kislev, he turns to Chanukah: following the Sfas Emes, the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Mikdash, so each home becomes a Beis HaMikdash and each Jew a kohen, bound to the hidden light of the future. He interprets the name Chashmonaim, explains why the Chanukah light may not be used while the Shabbos light may, and shows that the opening words of the psalm's blessing equal 'ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah' in gematria. Chanukah, like Rosh Hashanah, brings remembrance for the barren, physically and spiritually, and blessing means increase; 'children of your children' are chiddushei Torah that beget further chiddushim. He closes that the root of Chanukah is hallel and thanks.

en: Tehillim 128 depicts the warm, contented Jewish home, and 'Hashem will bless you from Zion' refers to the shul and beis medrash, the communal home from which warmth and Torah are brought into the house.
Since the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Mikdash, every Jew who lights them has his home become a Beis HaMikdash and himself become like a kohen.

Both the Shabbos light and the Chanukah light come from the hidden light, but on Shabbos a Jew rises to a higher world, while on Chanukah that light comes down into the weekday of exile, so it may not be used.
Chanukah is a time of remembrance for the barren, both for children and for those whose tefillah or Torah bears no fruit.
'Children of your children' alludes to chiddushei Torah that give rise to further chiddushim, the sign that a chiddush was accepted in Heaven.
The essence of Chanukah is hallel and thanks, which is why the Rambam places the laws of Hallel in the laws of Chanukah.

title.en: The Jewish home and Yerushalayim at Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav goes back from Tehillim 129 to 128 and, following Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch, describes the warm, contented Jewish home and the shul as the communal home. Turning to Chanukah, he brings the Sfas Emes that the Chanukah lights are a remembrance of the Mikdash, so that Yerushalayim comes to visit every Jewish home even on a weekday.

title.en: Matisyahu, the Mikdash and every Jew a kohen

summary.en: Using time, place and soul from Sefer Yetzirah, the Rav shows that Matisyahu is the soul of Chanukah and equals 'Beis HaMikdash' in gematria. He adds that each Jew becomes a kohen at Chanukah, tying this to the hidden light of Moshiach (Bnei Yissaschar), the Baal HaTurim on a kingdom of kohanim, and the Rambam that lighting the menorah needs no kohen.

title.en: The menorah's future light and the name Chashmonaim

summary.en: Following the Rokeach, the Rav explains that the menorah's lighting belongs to the light of the future, while its preparation still needs a kohen. He then brings the Chasam Sofer on the name Chashmonaim and adds his own reading: as Hashem answered Haman by adding Purim, He answered the Greeks, who wanted to abolish chodesh, Shabbos and milah, by adding ner Chanukah, alluded to in the letters of chashman.

title.en: Ner Chanukah and ner Shabbos as family mitzvos

summary.en: The Rav explains that ner Chanukah is a mitzvah on the family, 'a light for a man and his household', unlike tefillin, which fits the psalm's picture of the family around the table. Ner Shabbos is also a family obligation, and Shabbos itself is a Beis HaMikdash; the novelty of Chanukah is that this comes on a weekday.

title.en: Why the Chanukah light may not be used

summary.en: The Rav asks why one may not use the Chanukah light, which is from the hidden light, when the Shabbos light is also from the hidden light. He describes learning by the Shabbos candles and the Chazon Ish's Friday-night chiddush, and answers that on Shabbos a Jew is lifted to a higher world, while on Chanukah the future light comes down into the weekday of exile.

title.en: Light in the darkest time; ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Chanukah comes in the darkest time of the year, when the forces of impurity rule, and that today the public domain invades the Jewish home through television, radio and the internet, so one must light inside. Through ner Shabbos and ner Chanukah a Jew merits Zion even in exile, and he shows that the words of the blessing in the psalm equal 'ner Shabbos, ner Chanukah' in gematria.

title.en: Remembrance of the barren and blessing as increase

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Chanukah, like Rosh Hashanah, is a time of remembrance for the barren, in body and in spirit, including those whose tefillah or Torah is barren. Following the Maharal, the letters of bracha show increase, and Chanukah, which keeps adding, is a time of increase; the Bnei Yissaschar writes that one who makes chiddushei Torah fulfils pru u'rvu.

title.en: Achitofel's barren Torah and chiddushim that bear fruit

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's question on the Mishnah that David called Achitofel his rebbe for two things: why is this a kal vachomer? He answers that Achitofel's Torah was barren, while a chiddush that leads another to make a further chiddush makes its author a rebbe; this is 'children of your children', and Chanukah is a time for learning after lighting.

title.en: The root of Chanukah is hallel and thanks

summary.en: The Rav says the main mitzvah of Chanukah is hallel and thanks, as the Gemara says it was fixed for hallel and hoda'ah, and connects this to Mizmor Lesodah, the thanks that remains in the days of Moshiach. He notes that the Rambam waits until the laws of Chanukah to give the laws of Hallel, and closes that one must get used to thanking Hashem for every small thing.

catalogTitle: “לא איש אל כל ויכזב” - Hashem Knows Past Present and Future

oneLiner.en: The Rav contrasts Jewish emunah, which believes even what it cannot see, with Amalek's denial of what he saw, and shows from the Rambam and the pesukim that the Torah can never be changed, since Hashem is not a man who changes His mind.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by recalling that the Jewish belief in Moshe Rabbeinu and the Torah rests on what millions of Jews saw and heard at Har Sinai, passed down from generation to generation. Emunah in the full sense is believing what lies above human understanding, and since Hashem made the world with opposing forces, there is also a kefirah above understanding: denying what one sees. Amalek, who trembled at the splitting of the sea, still came to fight, the opposite of the Jews who believe even what they do not see. The Rav then explains that the nations, Christians and Muslims, accept the Torah but cannot keep it, and so claim Hashem changed His mind. From the Rambam in Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter nine and the pesukim, culminating in 'lo ish Kel vikazev', he shows the Torah can never change. He closes on why the nations hate the Jews, on censorship of sefarim, and on the security of Jewish emunah.

en: The Rav says the Jewish belief in the Torah rests on what a whole nation saw and heard at Har Sinai and passed down, which cannot be questioned.
Emunah means believing what is above the intellect; opposite it stands a kefirah above the intellect, refusing to believe even what one sees.
Amalek, who trembled at the splitting of the sea along with the other chiefs of Edom, still came to fight, denying what he saw.
The nations accept the Torah but cannot keep it, so they rationalize that Hashem changed His mind and gave them another Torah.
The Rambam, from explicit pesukim, establishes that the Torah stands forever, may not be added to or reduced, and that any prophet who says otherwise is a false prophet.
Hashem does not change His mind, because He knows what will be later; the pasuk says He is not a man who lies or changes his mind.
The Rav says the nations' hatred of the Jews comes from envy: deep down their thinking people know the truth but their pride and desires keep them from admitting it.

title.en: Emunah from Sinai and above the intellect

summary.en: The Rav recalls that belief in Moshe Rabbeinu and the Torah rests on what millions saw and heard at Sinai and passed down. He mentions the coming season of Purim and the war against Amalek, then explains that emunah means believing what is above the intellect, and that Hashem made every force of holiness with an opposing force.

title.en: Amalek denies what he sees

summary.en: Opposite emunah above the intellect stands a kefirah above the intellect: refusing to believe what one sees. The Rav explains that seeing is not believing, that the Jews at the sea believed even beyond what they saw, while Amalek, one of the terrified chiefs of Edom, came to fight anyway; Moshe Rabbeinu against Amalek is emunah against kefirah.

title.en: Why the nations accept the Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a fact witnessed by a multitude and passed down cannot be doubted, like the conquests of Alexander the Great, and the whole Jewish people everywhere has the same Torah and mitzvos. Therefore Christians and Muslims accept the Torah; he asks why they then have other religions and answers that they cannot keep it and rationalize that Hashem changed His mind.

title.en: The Torah can never change

summary.en: The Rav reads from the Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah chapter nine, that the Torah stands forever and nothing may be added or taken away, bringing the pesukim of 'lo sosef', 'lanu ul'vaneinu ad olam' and 'lo bashamayim hi'. A prophet who claims the mitzvos were temporary is a false prophet, and he ends with the pasuk that Hashem is not a man who lies or changes His mind, since He knows the future.

title.en: Why the nations hate the Jews

summary.en: The Rav says the learned among the nations know the truth but their pride and desires keep them from admitting it, and asks why they hate the Jews; he answers that it is envy. He describes how censors removed passages from the siddur, the Rambam and the Gemara, tells of converts who gave their lives for the truth, and closes with the security and joy of Jewish emunah in the Written and Oral Torah.

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the kapitel Shir Hamaalos Mimaamakim as a cry from the hidden depth of the Jewish soul, which sin never reaches, and as the song of a Jew who keeps waiting for the geulah through every disappointment.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Hirsch's view that this kapitel is the climax of the Shir Hamaalos: Hashem frees Jews even from their sins. Citing the Bnei Yissaschar that teshuvah does not help for the nations, he explains that Jews are children of Hashem, and the point of G-dliness in a Jew's heart is never touched by sin. He supports this from the Rambam on 'until he says I want', and from the thirty-nine lashes. He then reads the kapitel verse by verse: tachanunim as a request for an undeserved gift, forgiveness created before the world, the Jew's direct access to Hashem without intermediaries, and how forgiveness removes the barrier that blocks fear of Heaven. On 'kivisi Hashem' he speaks of daily disappointments in avodah and in the hope for Moshiach, the dates of the ketz that passed, the frum Jews whose machlokes delays the geulah, and the call to keep hoping.

en: This kapitel is the climax of the Shir Hamaalos: beyond saving Jews from physical troubles, Hashem frees them from their sins.
Jews are children of Hashem, and the point of G-dliness in the depth of a Jew's heart is never reached by sin; this depth is the 'maamakim' from which the Jew calls.
A Jew comes to Hashem for forgiveness directly, like a child to his father, without the intermediaries needed before a human king.
Sins form a barrier between a person and Hashem that blocks fear of Heaven; forgiveness removes it, which is why forgiveness leads to fear of Hashem.
A Jew must keep hoping after each disappointment, in his own avodah and in waiting for the geulah, like watchmen waiting for the morning.
Times for the ketz passed without the geulah because they were times of 'achishenah', dependent on merit, and the geulah was spoiled.

title.en: Why Hashem frees Jews from sin

summary.en: The Rav brings Hirsch's view that this kapitel is the climax of the Shir Hamaalos, since Hashem frees Jews even from their sins, and asks why. From the Bnei Yissaschar he shows that teshuvah does not help the nations, and explains that Jews are children of Hashem, carrying a point of G-dliness that sin does not touch.

title.en: The inner will and the depths

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam on forcing a person until he says 'I want', explaining that every Jew inwardly wants Hashem's will. He speaks of the hidden part of the Torah that the Arizal permitted to reveal, and of the thirty-nine lashes that do not reach the highest level of the soul, then reads 'mimaamakim' as calling from that depth.

title.en: Tachanunim: asking for an undeserved gift

summary.en: On 'Hashem shim'ah bekoli', the Rav brings Rashi that tachanunim means asking for an undeserved gift, and the Midrash of the treasure of matnas chinam shown to Moshe Rabbeinu, which opens only to one who knows nothing is due to him. On 'im avonos tishmor' he notes that even the greatest tzaddikim had a flaw.

title.en: Forgiveness before the world; no intermediary

summary.en: The Rav explains that since man is prone to sin from Adam on, forgiveness was created before the world. On 'ki imcha haselichah' he contrasts the intermediaries needed before a king, and the confession of the gentiles, with a Jew who comes straight to Hashem as a child, and reads Kayin's 'gadol avoni minso'.

title.en: Forgiveness so that You be feared

summary.en: The Rav brings the Berditchever's words that Hashem is full of mercy greater than man's sins, and explains 'lema'an tivareh': without forgiveness a sinner would despair and give himself over to this world. He then explains that sins are a barrier that keeps a person from feeling Hashem, and forgiveness removes it so he can fear Hashem.

title.en: Kivisi Hashem: hope after disappointment

summary.en: On 'kivisi Hashem' the Rav describes the great day when the whole world will recognize Hashem, and the daily and weekly disappointments of a Jew who resolves to serve Hashem and falls again. He tells how the Sassover Rebbe would resolve each morning to begin anew, and reads 'mishomrim laboker' as waiting for the personal and general geulah.

title.en: Waiting for Moshiach; be'itah and achishenah

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Yismach Moshe waited for Moshiach every moment, including the story of his son's arrival. He then brings the Gemara on 'be'itah achishenah' and the Gemara in Avodah Zarah about a certain year, explaining that the Tannaim's times were times of achishenah, and that at such a time the Satan accuses and brings troubles.

title.en: Dates of the ketz and the spoiled geulah

summary.en: The Rav goes through dates that were foretold for the geulah and brought great troubles instead, and says the geulah was spoiled not by the irreligious but by machlokes and lashon hara among frum Jews. He brings the Arizal's date for the great day of judgment, calls for preparing and self-correction, and ends with 'kivisi Hashem': after each disappointment one keeps waiting for the morning.

oneLiner.en: On the closing verses of Shir HaMa'alos 'MiMa'amakim', the Rav teaches that a Jew keeps hoping and waiting for Hashem and for the geulah even when every awaited 'morning' passes, and that one who takes shelter in Hashem is redeemed even beyond strict judgment.

abstract.en: The Rav reads 'Kivisi Hashem kivsa nafshi' as a call to keep hoping and praying even when a tefillah is not answered. 'Nafshi la-Hashem mishomrim laboker' is the waiting for the geulah: there is a fixed time that must come, and there are 'mornings' when it can come earlier. He speaks of Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid, of how little anyone knows about the order of the redemption, and of the Arizal's words about the year 5765. After stories of tzaddikim who foresaw the fall of Russia, he lists awaited dates that passed and answers that a Jew never gives up: 'Yachel Yisrael el Hashem'. Adam's sin and the Golden Calf were failures to wait. The chapter ends with pedus from sins: Hashem, like a king, can rise above judgment for one who takes shelter in Him, as the Akeidah, the extra verse of Tehillim 34, and the story of Rebbi and the ox show.

en: When a tefillah is not answered, a person must keep hoping to Hashem and keep praying.
'Mishomrim laboker' describes waiting for the geulah: a set time must come regardless, but there are 'mornings' when it can come earlier, and when one passes a Jew waits for the next.
Nobody knows exactly how the redemption will unfold; what is certain is the Torah's promise that it will be greater than anything that came before.
Even after many awaited dates have passed, a Jew does not give up hope; hoping, waiting and believing are the essence of Yiddishkeit and the tikkun of the world.
Adam's sin and the sin of the Golden Calf both came from not waiting, and a Jew's whole tikkun is to wait.
Beyond rescue from troubles, 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' speaks of redemption from sins, the greatest pedus.
Like a king who can pardon, Hashem can rise above strict judgment for one who throws himself upon Him and takes shelter in Him.

title.en: Keep hoping; waiting for the morning

summary.en: The Rav explains 'Kivisi Hashem kivsa nafshi': one who prayed and was not answered must keep hoping and praying. He reads 'mishomrim laboker' as waiting for the geulah, distinguishing a set time that must come (with the Ramban at the end of Haazinu) from earlier times when it can come.

title.en: Two Moshiachs and the unknown order

summary.en: The Rav distinguishes Moshiach ben Yosef, who can come any day, from Moshiach ben Dovid and the full geulah, and connects the two to Moshe Rabbeinu's two comings in this week's sedra. He adds that, as the Rambam says, nobody knows exactly how the redemption will happen.

title.en: The Torah's promise and the Arizal on 5765

summary.en: What is certain is the Torah's promise in Bechukosai and Nitzavim. The Rav cites the Arizal that a great day of judgment will come in 5765, urges taking it seriously, and explains why the Arizal's words carry weight: before Moshiach tzaddikim greater than their generation can appear.

title.en: Tzaddikim who foresaw Russia's fall

summary.en: The Rav tells of R' Elya Roth in Yerushalayim, who said Russia would soon crumble, and of the Stoliner Rebbe R' Yochanan, who said Russia would last seventy years. He adds R' Elya Roth's tradition that Christianity cannot last more than two thousand years, and a tzaddik's custom of wishing Jews a good year on the gentile New Year.

title.en: When the awaited morning passes

summary.en: The Rav lists awaited times that brought troubles instead of redemption: the Zohar's year 5408, the Malbim's calculation of 1914, a year in the 5700s, and 5746. He asks whether a Jew then gives up, and answers with 'Yachel Yisrael el Hashem': Yiddishkeit is hoping, waiting and believing.

title.en: Adam, the Calf and the Malbim: a Jew waits

summary.en: Hashem too waits impatiently to help His people. The Rav shows that Adam's sin was not waiting for Shabbos and the Golden Calf was not waiting for Moshe, so a Jew's tikkun is to wait. He tells how the Malbim explained to his students that the maskilim 'can do more' than he can.

title.en: Pedus from sins and the transfer of decrees

summary.en: The Rav explains that the chapter's last verse speaks of redemption from sins, greater than rescue from troubles. One who finds favor before Hashem can have his decrees transferred to another, as with the se'ir hamishtalei'ach, kaparos on Erev Yom Kippur, 'nasati koferecha Mitzrayim' and the ransom paid for a goring ox.

title.en: Rising above judgment: Tehillim 34 and the Akeidah

summary.en: Hashem runs the world by judgment, but like a king He reserves the right to pardon. The Rav shows this in Tehillim 34, whose alphabet maps the order of creation and judgment, while the extra verse 'Podeh Hashem nefesh avadav' stands outside it. He explains the Akeidah as chesed binding din, renewed each Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

title.en: Rebbi and the ox: asking asylum from Hashem

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara of the ox that fled to Rebbi and the suffering that followed, and a ba'al mussar's question why Rebbi was punished if he was right. The answer: one who asks asylum must be saved. A Midrash parable of a man who claimed to be the king's relative shows that whoever takes shelter in Hashem cannot be held guilty.

catalogTitle: שיר המעלות לדוד ה' לא גבה לבי

oneLiner.en: Through the last verses of Tehillim 130 and the opening of Tehillim 131, the Rav teaches that no tefilah is ever lost, that Jews keep hoping for the geulah through every disappointed date, and that Hashem redeems His children even beyond what they deserve.

abstract.en: The Rav continues Tehillim 130 with 'Kivisi Hashem... v'lidvaro hochalti'. Moshe Rabbeinu davened 515 tefillos and was told to stop one short; that missing tefilah is completed by the tefillos of Klal Yisrael, so one whose prayer is not answered keeps davening. From the Yitav Lev he shows that Hashem told Avraham about Sedom so that his unanswered tefilah would be stored for his children. Times of geulah pass without visible result, as with Achashverosh's and Daniel's calculations and the dates spoken of in later generations, yet a Jew waits for the next 'morning'. 'V'harbeh imo fedus' and 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' teach that Hashem can redeem even the unworthy, as at Purim, a great eis ratzon that must not be wasted on wild drunkenness. He closes on Tehillim 131: Dovid did not seek grandeur for himself, only for the Beis HaMikdash.

en: One tefilah was missing from Moshe Rabbeinu's 516, and the tefillos of Klal Yisrael over the generations add up to it; so one whose prayer is not answered keeps davening.
A tefilah that cannot help now is kept in reserve for a later time, as Hashem told Avraham about Sedom so his prayer would be stored for his descendants.
Times of geulah come and pass without a visible result, and even the greatest, like Daniel, did not understand the calculations; a Jew keeps waiting for the next morning.
'V'harbeh imo fedus' and 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' teach that when the time of geulah comes Hashem redeems Klal Yisrael even if they are not worthy.
Purim was a miracle of chesed beyond the people's deeds and is a greater eis ratzon than any other time, which the yetzer hara tries to waste on wild drunkenness.
Dovid HaMelech did not seek the grandeur of a king for himself, only for the Beis HaMikdash, and the Rav warns against building luxurious houses in galus.

title.en: Moshe's missing tefilah and davening again

summary.en: Resuming at 'Kivisi Hashem', the Rav brings that Moshe Rabbeinu davened 515 tefillos and was stopped one short, because Hashem knew what was better for Klal Yisrael; that missing tefilah is completed by Jews' tefillos over the generations, so one who is not answered must daven again.

title.en: Avraham's tefilah kept in reserve

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yitav Lev on 'hamechaseh ani me'Avraham': Hashem told Avraham about Sedom although his tefilah would not help, so that it would be stored for his descendants. He reads 'v'lidvaro hochalti' as waiting for Hashem's word in later times, and notes that times of geulah have passed without our understanding what happened.

title.en: Achashverosh's and Daniel's calculations

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara in Megillah that Achashverosh counted the seventy years, saw the Jews not redeemed and made his feast, because a goy cannot bear the Beis HaMikdash, and he applies this to the nations' attitude to Yerushalayim today. He adds that Daniel too erred in the calculation and was told the matters are sealed.

title.en: Pekidah, eis ratzon and the hidden ketz

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seventy years were a pekidah, an eis ratzon in which a little more davening, learning and ehrlichkeit can bring Moshiach early, while the fixed day is known only to Hashem. The Satan uses such times to recall sins, and this explains why Haman's decree came seventy years after the bowing to the image.

title.en: Dates that passed, and waiting for the morning

summary.en: The Rav describes the dates for which geulah was expected: the founding of the state, which he calls an imitation diamond with some advantages but nothing from the side of geulah; the year the Satmar Rav cried out to do teshuvah; and the date spoken of by the Arizal, for which one must prepare. He tells of the Blazhever Rav who turned pale at a joke that Moshiach had come, and reads 'nafshi la'Hashem mishomrim laboker' as waiting for morning after morning.

title.en: 'V'harbeh imo fedus': redemption beyond merit

summary.en: On 'yachel Yisrael el Hashem... v'harbeh imo fedus' the Rav brings that 'pedus' is written full here, alluding to the complete redemption of the third Beis HaMikdash, and that 'v'hu yifdeh es Yisrael mikol avonosav' means that when the time comes Hashem redeems even the unworthy. He describes Hashem's way of making a substitute, as with the se'ir la'azazel, kaparos, and 'nasati chofrecha Mitzrayim'.

title.en: The extra pei and Purim's chesed

summary.en: The Rav shows that two alphabetical chapters of Tehillim end with an extra verse of pedus after the alef-beis of reward and punishment: a higher conduct in which Hashem redeems His children even when they do not deserve it. Purim was such a miracle despite the people's sins, and the week's sedra shows the same with the machatzis hashekel atoning and the revealing of the thirteen middos.

title.en: Purim as an eis ratzon, and drinking

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Purim miracle came from Hashem's chesed, not the people's deeds, so on Purim one gives to whoever stretches out a hand, and it is a greater eis ratzon than any time of the year. He laments that the yetzer hara turns it into wild drunkenness, contrasts the Gemara's account of how the nations and the Jews behave when they drink, and discusses the views on drinking on Purim.

title.en: 'Lo gavah libi': Dovid's humility and fancy houses in galus

summary.en: The Rav begins Tehillim 131: Dovid HaMelech, unlike other kings, did not seek grandeur and luxury for himself, only for the Beis HaMikdash. From here he brings the Shelah and Sefer Chassidim, who warn against building fine stone houses in galus, and says a house should be comfortable for the family and for learning, while the Beis Hashem must be beautiful.
